1.pericope_label: Paul closes the argument from his own example, praises the Corinthians for keeping the traditions he delivered, and lays down the order of headship: Christ the head of every man, the man the head of the woman, God the head of Christ

schools.summary: John Gill says these words more properly close the preceding chapter than begin a new one, and refer to the rules therein laid down, which the apostle would have the Corinthians follow him in as he did Christ: that as he sought both in private and public, and more especially in his ministerial service, to do all things to the glory of God and not for his own popular applause, in which he imitated Christ, who sought not his own glory but the glory of him that sent him, so he would have them do all they did in the name of Christ; and that as he studied to exercise a conscience void of offence to God and man, in which he was a follower of Christ, who was holy in his nature and harmless and inoffensive in his conversation, so he was desirous that they should likewise be blameless and without offence until the day of Christ; and that whereas he endeavoured to please men in all things lawful and indifferent, he therein copied after Christ. The apostle prefaces what he had to say by way of commendation of them, Gill says, though some think that this is said in an ironical way, because there are many things both in this chapter and in the following part of this epistle delivered by way of reproof; but whoever considers the change of style will easily see that this must be spoken seriously here, and is designed to raise the attention to what he was about to say, and to prepare their minds to receive and take in good part what he should say by way of rebuke, since none could well be angry when he praised them for what was praiseworthy and reproved them for what was blamable. Though they were mindful of him, and retained in memory many things he had declared among them, and kept the ordinances as delivered to them, yet there were some things in which they were either ignorant or at least did not so well advert to, and needed to be put in mind of, Gill says; and as the apostle was very communicative of his knowledge in every point, he fails not to acquaint them with whatsoever might be instructive to their faith and a direction to their practice. John Calvin says that from this it appears how absurdly chapters are divided, inasmuch as this sentence is disjoined from what goes before, with which it ought to have been connected, and is joined to what follows, with which it has no connection; let us view this, then, as the close of the preceding chapter, since Paul had there brought forward his own example in confirmation of his doctrine. Here there are two things to be observed, Calvin says: first, that he prescribes nothing to others that he had not first practised himself, and secondly, that he directs himself and others to Christ as the only pattern of right acting. While it is the part of a good teacher to enjoin nothing in words but what he is prepared to practise in action, he must not at the same time be so austere as straightway to require from others everything that he does himself, as is the manner of the superstitious, Calvin says, for everything that they contract a liking for they impose also upon others, and would have their own example to be held absolutely as a rule. The world is also, of its own accord, inclined to a misdirected imitation, and after the manner of apes men strive to copy whatever they see done by persons of great influence, Calvin says; we see, however, how many evils have been introduced into the Church by this absurd desire of imitating all the actions of the saints without exception, and let us therefore maintain so much the more carefully this doctrine of Paul, that we are to follow men provided they take Christ as their grand model, that the examples of the saints may not tend to lead us away from Christ but rather to direct us to him. Calvin says Paul passes on now to another subject, to instruct the Corinthians what decorum ought to be observed in the sacred assemblies; for as a man's dress or gesture has in some cases the effect of disfiguring and in others of adorning him, so all actions are set off to advantage by decorum and are vitiated by the want of it, and much therefore depends upon decorum, not merely for securing for our actions gracefulness and beauty but also to accustom our minds to propriety. While this is true in a general way as to everything, it holds especially as to sacred things, Calvin says, for what contempt, and eventually what barbarism, will be incurred if we do not preserve dignity in the Church by conducting ourselves honourably and becomingly. In order to prepare them the more for obedience he commends at the outset their obedience in the past, Calvin says, inasmuch as they observed his ordinances; and by retaining this the Corinthians gave reason to hope that they would also in future be docile. It is surprising, however, that while he now bestows upon them this commendation he had previously blamed them for many things, Calvin says; the answer is that there were some that were infected with those vices which he had previously reproved, some with one and others with another, but that in the meantime the form which he had prescribed to them had been retained by the entire body, for there is nothing of inconsistency in saying that very many sins and of various kinds prevail among a particular people, some cheating, others plundering, some envying, others quarrelling, while at the same time, in respect of the public form of the Church, the institutions of Christ and his Apostles are maintained. It is necessary to speak of the word traditions for the purpose of replying to Papists, who arm themselves with this passage for the purpose of defending their traditions, Calvin says: it is a common maxim among them that the doctrine of the Apostles consists partly of writings and partly of traditions, and under this department they include not merely certain foolish superstitions and puerile ceremonies but also all kinds of gross abomination directly contrary to the plain word of God, and their tyrannical laws, which are mere torments to men's consciences; in this way there is nothing so foolish, nothing so absurd, nothing so monstrous, as not to have shelter under this pretext. Calvin does not deny that there were certain traditions of the Apostles that were not committed to writing, but he does not admit that they were parts of doctrine or related to things necessary for salvation: they were connected with order and government, for we know that every Church has liberty to frame for itself a form of government that is suitable and profitable for it, because the Lord has not prescribed anything definite. Thus Paul, the first founder of the Corinthian Church, had also framed for its regulation pious and seemly enactments, that all things should be done decently and in order, Calvin says; but what has this to do with the silly ceremonies to be seen in Popery, or with a worse than Jewish superstition, or with a tyranny worthy of Phalaris by which they torture miserable consciences, or with so many monstrous rites of idolatry? The foundation of all right enactment was to observe the moderation that Paul made use of, Calvin says. On the headship, Calvin says it is an old proverb that evil manners beget good laws: as the rite here treated of had not been previously called in question, Paul had given no enactment respecting it, and the error of the Corinthians was the occasion of his showing what part it was becoming to act in this matter. With the view of proving that it is an unseemly thing for women to appear in a public assembly with their heads uncovered, and on the other hand for men to pray or prophesy with their heads covered, he sets out with noticing the arrangements that are divinely established, Calvin says, and points out four gradations. God occupies the first place, and Christ holds the second: how so? Inasmuch as he has in our flesh made himself subject to the Father, for apart from this, being of one essence with the Father, he is his equal; let us therefore bear it in mind that this is spoken of Christ as mediator, and that he is inferior to the Father inasmuch as he assumed our nature, Calvin says. There is somewhat more of difficulty in what follows, Calvin says, for here the man is placed in an intermediate position between Christ and the woman, so that Christ is not the head of the woman; yet the same Apostle teaches us elsewhere that there is neither male nor female. Why then does he make a distinction here which in that passage he does away with? Calvin answers that the solution of this depends on the connection in which the passages occur: when he says that there is no difference between the man and the woman he is treating of Christ's spiritual kingdom, in which individual distinctions are not regarded or made any account of, for it has nothing to do with the body and nothing to do with the outward relationships of mankind, but has to do solely with the mind; in the meantime, however, he does not disturb civil order or honorary distinctions, which cannot be dispensed with in ordinary life. Here, on the other hand, he reasons respecting outward propriety and decorum, which is a part of ecclesiastical polity, Calvin says.

Matthew Henry says that Paul, having answered the cases put to him, proceeds in this chapter to the redress of grievances; the first verse of the chapter is put, by those who divided the epistle into chapters, as a preface to the rest of the epistle, but seems to have been a more proper close to the last, in which he had enforced the cautions he had given against the abuse of liberty by his own example, and the way of speaking in the next verse looks like a transition to another subject. But whether it more properly belong to this or the last chapter, it is plain from it that Paul not only preached such doctrine as they ought to believe but led such a life as they ought to imitate, Henry says: be imitators of me, that is, live as you see me live; and ministers are likely to preach most to the purpose when they can press their hearers to follow their example. Yet would not Paul be followed blindly neither, Henry says: he encourages neither implicit faith nor obedience, and he would be followed himself no further than he followed Christ, for Christ's pattern is a copy without a blot, and so is no man's else; we should follow no leader further than he follows Christ, and apostles should be left by us when they deviate from the example of their Master. He begins with a commendation of what was praiseworthy in them, Henry says, and many of them, it is probable, did this in the strictest sense of the expression, so that he takes occasion to address the body of the church under this good character; and the body might in the main have continued to observe the ordinances and institutions of Christ, though in some things they deviated from and corrupted them. When we reprove what is amiss in any, it is very prudent and fit to commend what is good in them, Henry says, for it will show that the reproof is not from ill-will and a humour of censuring and finding fault, and it will therefore procure the more regard to it. He lays the foundation for his reprehension by asserting the superiority of the man over the woman, Henry says: Christ, in his mediatorial character and glorified humanity, is at the head of mankind, not only first of the kind but Lord and Sovereign, having a name above every name, though in this high office and authority he has a superior, God being his head; and as God is the head of Christ, and Christ the head of the whole human kind, so the man is the head of the two sexes, not indeed with such dominion as Christ has over the kind, or God over the man Christ Jesus, but a superiority and headship he has, and the woman should be in subjection and not assume or usurp the man's place. This is the situation in which God has placed her, Henry says, and for that reason she should have a mind suited to her rank and not do anything that looks like an affectation of changing places. Something like this the women of the church of Corinth seem to have been guilty of, who were under inspiration and prayed and prophesied even in their assemblies, Henry says; it is indeed an apostolical canon that the women should keep silence in the churches, which some understand without limitation, as if a woman under inspiration also must keep silence, and others with a limitation, that though a woman might not from her own abilities pretend to teach or so much as question and debate anything in the church, yet when under inspiration the case was altered and she had liberty to speak; or that though she might not preach even by inspiration, because teaching is the business of a superior, yet she might pray or utter hymns by inspiration even in the public assembly, and did not show any affectation of superiority over the man by such acts of public worship. It is plain the apostle does not in this place prohibit the thing but reprehend the manner of doing it, Henry says, and yet he might utterly disallow the thing and lay an unlimited restraint on the woman in another part of the epistle, these things not being contradictory; it is to his present purpose to reprehend the manner wherein the women prayed and prophesied in the church, without determining in this place whether they did well or ill in praying or prophesying, for the manner of doing a thing enters into the morality of it, and we must not only be concerned to do good but that the good we do be well done. John Lightfoot, annotating from the rabbinic sources, cites the rule that men might show themselves reverent and ashamed before God, and unworthy with an open face to behold him, and quotes the saying that the wise men and the scholars of the wise men are not to pray unless they be covered.

Adam Clarke summarises the chapter: the apostle reprehends the Corinthians for several irregularities in their manner of conducting public worship, the men praying or prophesying with their heads covered and the women with their heads uncovered, contrary to custom, propriety and decency; he gives reasons why they should act differently; they are also reproved for their divisions and heresies, and for the irregular manner in which they celebrated the Lord's Supper; the proper manner of celebrating this holy rite is laid down by the apostle; and directions are given for a profitable receiving of the Lord's Supper and for avoiding the dangerous consequences of communicating unworthily. On the first verse Clarke says it certainly belongs to the preceding chapter, and is here out of all proper place and connection. It appears that the apostle had previously given them a variety of directions relative to the matters mentioned here, Clarke says, and that some had paid strict attention to them and others had not, and that contentions and divisions were the consequences, which he here reproves and endeavours to rectify. While Paul and Apollos had preached among them they had undoubtedly prescribed everything that was necessary to be observed in the Christian worship, Clarke says, but it is likely that those who joined in idol festivals wished also to introduce something relative to the mode of conducting the idol worship into the Christian assembly, which they might think was an improvement on the apostle's plan. The head of every man is Christ: the apostle is speaking particularly of Christianity and its ordinances, Clarke says, and Christ is the Head or Author of this religion, and is the creator, preserver and Lord of every man; the man also is the lord or head of the woman, and the Head or Lord of Christ, as Mediator between God and man, is God the Father. Here is the order, Clarke says: God sends his Son Jesus Christ to redeem man, Christ comes and lays down his life for the world, every man who receives Christianity confesses that Jesus Christ is Lord to the glory of God the Father, and every believing woman will acknowledge that God has placed her in a dependence on and subjection to the man; so far there is no difficulty in this passage. John Wesley says the apostle does not seem to have given them any order before concerning this. The head of every man means particularly every believer, Wesley says, and Christ as he is Mediator acts in all things subordinately to his Father; but we can no more infer that they are not of the same divine nature, because God is said to be the head of Christ, than that man and woman are not of the same human nature, because the man is said to be the head of the woman.

Albert Barnes says the first verse of this chapter properly belongs to the preceding and is the conclusion of the discussion the apostle had been carrying on, having been improperly separated from that chapter, and in reading should be read in connexion with it; the remainder of the chapter is properly divided into two parts, a discussion respecting the impropriety of a woman's praying or prophesying with her head uncovered, and a reproof of their irregularities in the observance of the Lord's Supper. In regard to the first, Barnes says it seems probable that some of the women who, on pretence of being inspired, had prayed or prophesied in the Corinthian church, had cast off their veils after the manner of the heathen priestesses, and this indecent and improper custom the apostle reproves. Be ye followers of me means imitate my example in the matter now under discussion, Barnes says: as I deny myself, as I seek to give no offence to any one, as I endeavour not to alarm the prejudices of others but in all things to seek their salvation, so do you; and even as I also am of Christ means, I make Christ my example, he is my model in all things, and this is the only safe example, for if we follow this we can never go astray. Paul always chose to commend Christians when it could be done, and never seemed to suppose that such praise would be injurious to them, Barnes says, and on this occasion he was the more ready to praise them because there were some things in which he would have occasion to reprove them. That ye remember me in all things means that you are disposed to regard my authority and seek my direction in all matters pertaining to the good order of the church, Barnes says, and there can be little doubt that they had consulted him in their letter about the proper manner in which a woman ought to demean herself if she was called upon, under the influence of divine inspiration, to utter anything in public: the question seems to have been whether, since she was inspired, it was proper for her to retain the marks of her inferiority of rank and remain covered, or whether the fact of her inspiration released her from that obligation. The word rendered ordinances does not refer to anything that had been handed down from a former generation, as the word tradition now usually signifies, Barnes says, but means that which had been delivered to them by the apostles, who had delivered certain doctrines or rules respecting the good order and government of the church. The word head in the Scriptures is designed often to denote master, ruler, chief, Barnes says, with many instances in the Old Testament and in the New; here it means that Christ is the Ruler, Director or Lord of the Christian man, a truth to be regarded in all their feelings and arrangements, and every Christian should recollect the relation in which he stands to him, as one that is fitted to produce the strictest decorum and a steady sense of subordination. Charles Ellicott says a new subject is here introduced and occupies the next fifteen verses: the exhortation of the previous verse probably recalled to the Apostle's mind that to a certain extent the Corinthians did follow his teaching and example, and had possibly in their letter, to which he was now replying, boasted of their obedience, so that the rebuke which he is about to administer is, with characteristic courtesy, introduced with words of commendation. While there is a likeness in form in the original between the words imitators and remember, the latter is weaker in its significance, Ellicott says: he exhorts them to be imitators, but praises them only for bearing him in mind to the extent of obeying certain practical directions which he had given them; and the word ordinances, or traditions, here refers to matters of Christian discipline. The subject treated of, namely the uncovering of their heads by women in assemblies for worship, was of ephemeral moment, and as we all now would regard it of trivial importance, Ellicott says; every circumstance, however, which could in the least degree cause the principles of Christianity to be perverted or misunderstood by the heathen world was of vital importance in those early days of the Church, and hence we find the Apostle, who most fearlessly taught the principles of Christian liberty, condemning most earnestly every application of those principles which might be detrimental to the best interests of the Christian faith. To feel bound to assert your liberty in every detail of social and political life is to cease to be free, Ellicott says: the very liberty becomes a bondage. The Apostle does not merely treat of the outward practice on which his advice has been sought, Ellicott says, but proceeds to lay down the principles which are opposed to that absolute and essential equality which found its expression in the practice of women uncovering their heads in public assemblies; the allusion here is not to Christ as the Head of the whole human race and of all things, but as the Head of the Body, the Christian Church. This thought introduces the general argument regarding the practical subordination of woman, Ellicott says, by reminding the Corinthians that though there is in the Church a perfect spiritual equality, yet that it is an equality which is of order and not of disorder, an equality which can only be preserved by remembering that each is not an isolated irresponsible atom but a part of an organic whole: there is a Head to the Church, therefore it is not a machine composed of various parts but a body consisting of various members, and as there is a subordination of the whole body to Christ, so there is in that body a subordination of woman to man. The last clause gives completeness to the thought, as is St. Paul's custom, Ellicott says: as the Head of the Church, that is, as the man Christ Jesus, Christ is subordinate to the Father, and indeed perhaps the idea is carried farther into the mystery of the divine nature itself, as consisting of three Persons co-eternal and co-equal, yet being designated with an unvarying sequence as first and second and third. A.T. Robertson says imitators of me means in the principle of considerate love as shown in the preceding chapters, and in so far as Paul is himself an imitator of Christ; the preacher is a leader and is bound to set an example or pattern for others, and this verse clearly belongs to the preceding chapter and not to chapter eleven. On hold fast the traditions, Robertson says the word means merely something handed on from one to another, and the thing handed on may be bad, as in Matthew, and contrary to the will of God, or it may be wholly good as here; there is a constant conflict between the new and the old in science, medicine, law, theology, and the obscurantist rejects all the new and holds to the old both true and untrue, whereas new truth must rest upon old truth and is in harmony with it. But I would have you know is censure in contrast to the praise in the previous verse, Robertson says; and the head of Christ is God is rather, God is the head of Christ, since the noun is anarthrous and predicate.

John Chrysostom says that, having completed the discourse concerning the idol-sacrifices as became him, and having rendered it most perfect in all respects, the apostle proceeds to another thing which also itself was a complaint, but not so great a one; for it is his manner, as Chrysostom has said before, not to set down all the heavy accusations continuously, but to intersperse them and to give the hearer breathing space between the graver charges, so that the reader may not be overwhelmed. Chrysostom accordingly treats the matter of the veil as a lesser fault following a greater, and notes that Paul begins with commendation before he passes to reproof.

debates: Whether the first verse belongs to this chapter: Calvin calls the division absurd, since the sentence is cut off from what it belongs to and joined to what it has no connection with; Clarke, Barnes, Robertson and Gill all say plainly that it closes the preceding chapter; Henry alone declines to decide, noting only that the dividers made it a preface while it seems a better close, and adding that either way the point stands

What the traditions Paul commends are: Calvin uses the word to answer the Papists, conceding unwritten apostolic traditions but confining them to order and government and denying that they were doctrine or necessary to salvation; Barnes and Ellicott say the word means what the apostles delivered, not what a former generation handed down, and refer it to matters of discipline; Robertson treats the word without polemic as merely something handed on, good or bad according to its content, and turns it into a general observation about the obscurantist who holds to the old both true and untrue

How this passage stands with the equality taught in Galatians: Calvin divides the spheres, that there Paul treats the spiritual kingdom where external qualities are not regarded, while here he treats outward propriety, which is part of ecclesiastical polity; Ellicott makes the equality itself ordered, an equality of order and not of disorder, so that the Church is a body of members and not a machine of parts; Henry keeps the superiority but limits it, denying that the man's headship is a dominion like Christ's over mankind or God's over the man Christ Jesus

Whether the last clause touches the divine nature: Calvin restricts it to Christ as mediator, inferior as having assumed our nature and otherwise of one essence and equal; Wesley argues from the parallel, that a difference of nature can no more be inferred here than between man and woman; Ellicott alone suggests the thought may be carried further into the mystery of the divine nature itself, three Persons co-eternal and co-equal yet named in an unvarying sequence; Robertson corrects the rendering, that since the noun is anarthrous and predicate it is God who is the head of Christ
outliers: Calvin's warning against misdirected imitation, that men strive after the manner of apes to copy whatever they see done by persons of great influence, and that many evils have entered the Church by this desire to imitate all the actions of the saints
Ellicott's principle that to feel bound to assert your liberty in every detail of social and political life is to cease to be free, the very liberty becoming a bondage
Henry's image that Christ's pattern is a copy without a blot and no man's else is, so that apostles should be left when they deviate from their Master
Clarke's conjecture that those who had joined in idol festivals wished to import something of the manner of idol worship into the Christian assembly, thinking it an improvement on the apostle's plan
Chrysostom's observation that Paul deliberately does not set down all the heavy accusations continuously, but places a lesser complaint after a greater
Calvin's aside that the tyranny exercised over consciences by such traditions is worthy of Phalaris
Robertson's remark that new truth must rest upon old truth and is in harmony with it, against the obscurantist who rejects all the new

4.pericope_label: Every man praying or prophesying covered dishonours his head, and every woman uncovered dishonours hers, being as one shaven; if she will not be covered let her be shorn, and if that is a shame, let her be covered

schools.summary: John Gill says this is to be understood of praying and prophesying in public and not in private, and not to be restrained to the person that is the mouth of the congregation to God in prayer, or who preaches to the people in the name of God, but to be applied to every individual person that attends public worship, that joins in prayer with the minister and hears the word preached by him, which is meant by prophesying; for not foretelling future events is here meant, but explaining the word of God, the prophecies of the Old Testament or any part of Scripture, unless singing of psalms should rather be designed, since that is sometimes expressed by prophesying. Gill cites the company of prophets coming down from the high place with a psaltery and a tabret and a pipe and a harp before them, who should prophesy, and notes that the Targum renders it, they shall sing praise, upon which Kimchi observes that it is as if it were said their prophecy shall be songs and praises to God, spoken by the Holy Ghost. John Calvin says there are two propositions here, the first relating to the man and the other to the woman: the man commits an offence against Christ his head if he covers it, because he is subject to Christ with this understanding, that he is to hold the first place in the government of the house, for the father of the family is like a king in his own house, so that the glory of God shines forth in him in consequence of the authority with which he is invested; if he covers his head he lets himself down from that preeminence which God had assigned to him, so as to be in subjection, and thus the honour of Christ is infringed upon. For example, Calvin says, if the person whom the prince has appointed as his lieutenant does not know how to maintain his proper station, and instead of this exposes his dignity to contempt on the part of persons in the lowest station, does he not bring dishonour upon his prince? In like manner, if the man does not keep his own station, if he is not subject to Christ in such a way as to preside over his own family with authority, he obscures to that extent the glory of Christ, which shines forth in the well regulated order of marriage. Calvin takes prophesying to mean declaring the mysteries of God for the edification of the hearers, and praying to mean preparing a form of prayer and taking the lead of all the people, which is the part of the public teacher, for Paul is not arguing here as to every kind of prayer but as to solemn prayer in public. Let us, however, bear in mind that in this matter the error is merely in so far as decorum is violated and the distinction of rank which God has established is broken in upon, Calvin says: we must not be so scrupulous as to look upon it as a criminal thing for a teacher to have a cap on his head when addressing the people from the pulpit, for Paul means nothing more than that it should appear that the man has authority and the woman is under subjection, and this is secured when the man uncovers his head in the view of the Church, though he should afterwards put on his cap again from fear of catching cold; in fine, the rule to be observed here is decorum, and if that is secured Paul requires nothing farther. On the woman Calvin says the proposition is that women ought to be covered when they pray or prophesy, otherwise they dishonour their head; for as the man honours his head by showing his liberty, so the woman by showing her subjection, and hence, on the other hand, if the woman uncovers her head she shakes off subjection, involving contempt of her husband. It may seem, however, to be superfluous for Paul to forbid the woman to prophesy with her head uncovered while elsewhere he wholly prohibits women from speaking in the Church, Calvin says: it would not therefore be allowable for them to prophesy even with a covering upon their head, and hence it follows that it is to no purpose that he argues here as to a covering. It may be replied, Calvin says, that the Apostle, by here condemning the one, does not commend the other, for when he reproves them for prophesying with their head uncovered he at the same time does not give them permission to prophesy in some other way, but rather delays his condemnation of that vice to another passage, namely the fourteenth chapter; in this reply there is nothing amiss, though at the same time it might suit sufficiently well to say that the Apostle requires women to show their modesty not merely in a place in which the whole Church is assembled, but also in any more dignified assembly, either of matrons or of men, such as are sometimes convened in private houses. He now maintains from other considerations that it is unseemly for women to have their heads bare, Calvin says: nature abhors it, and to see a woman shaven is a spectacle that is disgusting and monstrous, whence we infer that the woman should be covered. Should any one now object that her hair is enough, as being a natural covering, Paul says that it is not, for it is such a covering as requires another thing to be made use of for covering it, Calvin says; and hence a conjecture is drawn, with some appearance of probability, that women who had beautiful hair were accustomed to uncover their heads for the purpose of showing off their beauty. It is not therefore without good reason that Paul, as a remedy for this vice, sets before them the opposite idea, that they be regarded as remarkable for unseemliness rather than for what is an incentive to lust, Calvin concludes.

John Lightfoot, on the words let her also be shorn, states the objection directly: if she be not veiled, let her be shorn; yea, rather you will say, let her go with her hair loose, for it was given her for a covering by nature; and he asks whether the apostle will suffer this. His annotation belongs to the Horae Hebraicae, in which the rabbinic material on veiling and on the shaving of women is set beside the apostle's argument; both Clarke and Barnes send their readers to him by name at this very point, Clarke saying that there is much in Lightfoot on the Jewish canon that a man should be veiled when he prays, and Barnes citing him for the proof that a woman should not appear in public unless she was veiled.

Adam Clarke says that praying or prophesying means any person who engages in public acts in the worship of God, whether prayer, singing or exhortation, for we learn from the apostle himself that to prophesy signifies to speak unto men to edification, exhortation and comfort, and this comprehends all that we understand by exhortation, or even preaching. Having his head covered, that is with his cap or turban on, dishonours his head, Clarke says, because the head being covered was a sign of subjection, and while he was employed in the public ministration of the word he was to be considered as a representative of Christ, on which account his being veiled would be improper. This decision of the apostle was in point blank hostility to the canons of the Jews, Clarke says, for they would not suffer a man to pray unless he was veiled, for which they gave this reason, that he should veil himself to show that he is ashamed before God and unworthy with open face to behold him; and Clarke adds that there is much in Lightfoot on this point. Whatever may be the meaning of praying and prophesying in respect to the man, they have precisely the same meaning in respect to the woman, Clarke says, so that some women at least, as well as some men, might speak to others to edification and exhortation and comfort; and this kind of prophesying or teaching was predicted by Joel and referred to by Peter, and had there not been such gifts bestowed on women the prophecy could not have had its fulfilment. The only difference marked by the apostle was that the man had his head uncovered because he was the representative of Christ, and the woman had hers covered because she was placed by the order of God in a state of subjection to the man, and because it was a custom both among the Greeks and Romans, and among the Jews an express law, that no woman should be seen abroad without a veil, Clarke says: this was and is a common custom through all the east, and none but public prostitutes go without veils, so that if a woman should appear in public without a veil she would dishonour her head, her husband, and must appear like those women who had their hair shorn off as the punishment of whoredom or adultery. Tacitus informs us, Clarke says, that considering the greatness of the population adulteries were very rare among the Germans, and when any woman was found guilty she was punished in this way, that having cut off her hair and stripped her before her relatives, her husband turned her out of doors; and we know that the woman suspected of adultery was ordered by the law of Moses to be stripped of her veil. Women reduced to a state of servitude or slavery had their hair cut off, Clarke says, as we learn from Achilles Tatius, where Clitophon says concerning Leucippe that she was sold for a slave, she dug in the ground, and her hair being shorn off her head was deprived of its ornament. It was also the custom among the Greeks to cut off their hair in time of mourning, Clarke says, citing Euripides, where Admetus, ordering a common mourning for his wife Alcestis, says, I order a general mourning for this woman, let the hair be shorn off and a black garment put on. Propriety and decency of conduct are the points which the apostle seems more especially to have in view, Clarke says: as a woman who dresses loosely or fantastically even in the present day is considered a disgrace to her husband, because suspected to be not very sound in her morals, so in those ancient times a woman appearing without a veil would be considered in the same light. If she will not wear a veil in the public assemblies, let her be shorn, let her carry a public badge of infamy, Clarke says; but if to be shorn or shaven would appear, as it must, a badge of infamy, then let her by all means wear a veil. Even in mourning it was considered disgraceful to be obliged to shear off the hair, Clarke adds, and lest they should lose this ornament of their heads the women contrived to evade the custom by cutting off the ends of it only, as Euripides says of Helen, who should have shaved her head on account of the death of her sister, see how she cuts off only the very points of her hair, that she may preserve her beauty, and is just the same woman as before. In Hindostan a woman cuts off her hair at the death of her husband as a token of widowhood, Clarke reports from Ward's Customs, but this is never performed by a married woman, whose hair is considered an essential ornament; and the veil of the Hindoo women is nothing more than the garment brought over the face, which is always very carefully done by the higher classes of women when they appear in the streets. John Wesley says praying or prophesying means speaking by the immediate power of God, and that with his head covered means either with a veil or with long hair; St. Paul seems to mean that as in these eastern nations veiling the head is a badge of subjection, so a man who prays or prophesies with a veil on his head reflects a dishonour on Christ, whose representative he is. Every woman who, under an immediate impulse of the Spirit, for then only was a woman suffered to speak in the church, prays or prophesies without a veil on her face, as it were disclaims subjection and reflects dishonour on man, her head, Wesley says, for it is the same in effect as if she cut her hair short and wore it in the distinguishing form of the men; and in those ages men wore their hair exceeding short, as appears from the ancient statues and pictures. If she will throw off the badge of subjection, let her appear with her hair cut like a man's, Wesley says; but if it be shameful for a woman to appear thus in public, especially in a religious assembly, let her for the same reason keep on her veil.

Albert Barnes says that in the Old Testament prophetesses are not unfrequently mentioned, Miriam and Deborah and Huldah and Noadiah, and in the New Testament Anna, so that there were females in the early Christian church who corresponded to those known among the Jews as endowed with the inspiration of the Holy Spirit; what their precise office was, and what the nature of the public services in which they were engaged, is not however known, though it is clear that they prayed and apparent that they publicly expounded the will of God. As the presumption is that they were inspired, Barnes says, their example is no warrant now for females to take part in the public services of worship unless they also give evidence that they are under the influence of inspiration, and the more especially as the apostle Paul has expressly forbidden their becoming public teachers; if it is now pleaded from this example that women should speak and pray in public, yet it should be just so far only as this example goes, and only when they have the qualifications that the early prophetesses had. It may be further observed, Barnes says, that the fact that Paul here mentions the custom of women praying or speaking publicly in the church does not prove that it was right or proper, his immediate object being not to consider whether the practice was itself right but to condemn the manner of its performance as a violation of all the proper rules of modesty and of subordination, since on another occasion in this very epistle he fully condemns the practice in any form. With her head uncovered means with the veil removed which she usually wore, Barnes says, and it would seem from this that the women removed their veils and wore their hair dishevelled when they pretended to be under the influence of divine inspiration; this was the case with the heathen priestesses, and in so doing the Christian women imitated them, on which account if on no other Paul declares the impropriety of this conduct. It was besides a custom among ancient females, and one strictly enjoined by the traditional laws of the Jews, that a woman should not appear in public unless she was veiled, Barnes says, referring the reader to Lightfoot for the proof; and the veil is a token of modesty and of subordination, regarded among Jews and everywhere as an emblem of her sense of inferiority of rank and station, so that to remove it is to remove the appropriate mark of such subordination and is a public act by which she shows dishonour to the man. Charles Ellicott says the reference is to public prayer and teaching, the word prophesying being used in its less restricted sense, and that the Apostle probably does not allude to any actual case in Corinth where a man had taken part in a religious meeting with covered head; the Greek practice was for men to have their heads uncovered when joining in religious ceremonies, and to this practice St. Paul would incline, as being the national custom of the country and as also being typical of the distinction between the sexes which he has just laid down. The Apostle's teaching on this subject is a remarkable illustration of how completely he had overcome his old Jewish prejudice, and how the whole of his nature had become leavened with the freedom of the gospel, Ellicott says, for it was the custom amongst the Jews for the man to pray with covered head, and the face veiled with the Tallith, as an expression of his unworthiness to speak face to face with God. It was a profound insight into human nature which enabled the Apostle to realise how an external symbol would infallibly tend to modify doctrine, and how thus the perpetuating of such a custom in the Christian Church might have hindered the full recognition of the great truth of the personal and direct communication of every individual soul with the Father, Ellicott says. He dishonours his own head inasmuch as it is the part of his body from which Christ has taken his title as Head of the Body, the Church, and thus he dishonours his spiritual Head, Ellicott says. From the hypothetical case of the man praying with covered head, which was mentioned first for the sake of introducing the antithesis, the Apostle comes now to the actual case of which he has to treat, the woman uncovering her head, Ellicott says. At first sight the permission here implied for a woman to pray and teach in public may seem at variance with the teaching where she is commanded to observe silence, and the injunction that women should not teach, Ellicott says; in those passages, however, it is the public meeting of the whole Church that is spoken of, and in such the women were to be silent, but the meetings spoken of here, though public as distinguished from the private devotions of individuals, were probably only smaller gatherings. It has been suggested by some writers that the command elsewhere does forbid the practice which is here assumed to be allowable only for the sake of argument, Ellicott says; but surely St. Paul would not have occupied himself and his readers here with the elaborate and merely forensic discussion of the conditions under which certain functions were to be performed which he was about subsequently to condemn as not allowable under any restriction whatever? Both among Jews and Greeks the long tresses of a woman were her glory, Ellicott says, and only in times of mourning, or when convicted of shameful sin, was a woman to have her hair cut short; here again the word head must be taken in its double significance, for a woman with uncovered head dishonours that head itself by making it in the sight of others the type of a shame which is really not hers, and as her head typically is her husband, she dishonours him also. The force of the argument about being shorn depends on the fact that a woman's head being uncovered would be regarded by others as implying the same shame as was indicated by her hair being cut short or altogether removed, Ellicott says: it is as if the Apostle said, if a woman insists on her right to pray and speak in an assembly with uncovered head, let her carry out this principle to its logical result, let her insist on her right to have her hair cut short so as to show her equality with man, and what would be thought of her then? No woman with a spark of shame in her would think of doing that; accordingly you admit that this principle of sexual equality does not apply in all such matters, and it is illogical to argue in favour of any general principle as if it were of universal obligation when you yourselves admit that it is not applicable in some cases. A.T. Robertson says that having his head covered is literally having a veil down from the head, and that it is not certain whether the Jews at this time used the fringed shawl as they did later; Virgil says, and our heads are shrouded before the altar with a Phrygian vestment, while the Greeks, both men and women, remained bareheaded in public prayer, and this usage Paul commends for the men. With her head unveiled is an associative instrumental case of manner, Robertson says, and probably some of the women had violated this custom: amongst Greeks only the courtesans, so numerous in Corinth, went about unveiled, while slave-women wore the shaven head, which was also a punishment of the adulteress. It is public praying and prophesying that the Apostle here has in mind, Robertson says, and he does not here condemn the act but the breach of custom which would bring reproach; a woman convicted of adultery had her hair shorn, and the Justinian code prescribed shaving the head for an adulteress whom the husband refused to receive after two years, so that Paul does not tell Corinthian Christian women to put themselves on a level with courtesans. Let her also be shorn is an aorist middle imperative, let her cut her hair close, a single act by the woman, Robertson says; and clearly Paul uses such strong language because of the effect on a woman's reputation in Corinth by conduct that proclaimed her a lewd woman, for social custom varied in the world then as now, but there was no alternative in Corinth.

debates: Whether women might pray or prophesy in the assembly at all: Clarke argues they might, since the words mean the same for both sexes and the gift was foretold by Joel and claimed by Peter, so that without such gifts to women the prophecy could not have been fulfilled; Ellicott resolves the tension with the commands of silence by the size of the gathering, and expressly rejects the view that Paul argues only for the sake of argument; Calvin takes that rejected view, holding that in condemning the manner Paul does not commend the act but defers his censure to the fourteenth chapter; Barnes agrees with Calvin and adds that the example gives no warrant now unless the same evidence of inspiration appears; Wesley allows it only under an immediate impulse of the Spirit; Robertson says Paul condemns not the act but the breach of custom

How wide praying and prophesying are: Clarke takes prophesying from Paul's own definition as speaking to edification, exhortation and comfort, comprehending preaching; Gill applies the words to every worshipper present and not merely to the one who leads, and allows that prophesying may even mean the singing of psalms, citing the Targum and Kimchi; Calvin restricts praying to the framing of public prayer by the teacher and prophesying to declaring the mysteries of God, and says Paul is not arguing about every kind of prayer but about solemn public prayer; Ellicott takes the word in its less restricted sense

What the covered head meant before Paul ruled on it: Ellicott and Clarke both note that the ruling reverses Jewish practice, in which the man prayed veiled in the Tallith to confess his unworthiness to look on God, Clarke calling the decision point blank hostility to the canons of the Jews; Robertson supplies the Greek custom of praying bareheaded and doubts whether the Jews yet used the fringed shawl at all, quoting Virgil for the Roman practice of the covered head
outliers: Ellicott's insight that an external symbol will infallibly tend to modify doctrine, so that keeping the veiled head might have obscured the direct communication of every soul with the Father
Robertson's conclusion from the Corinthian evidence that Paul is not telling Christian women to put themselves on a level with courtesans

Clarke's parade of witnesses to the shorn head, Tacitus on the German husband who cut off his wife's hair and expelled her, Achilles Tatius on the slave-woman shorn of the ornament of her head, and Euripides on Helen cutting off only the very points of her hair to preserve her beauty

Ellicott's reductio, that a woman claiming the right to speak uncovered should on the same principle claim the right to crop her hair, and that it is illogical to press a general principle as universal when you yourselves admit exceptions

Calvin's insistence on proportion, that it would be no crime for a teacher to wear a cap in the pulpit provided he uncovers in view of the Church, even if he puts it on again for fear of catching cold
Lightfoot's objection that the woman might simply wear her hair loose, nature having given it for a covering, and his question whether the apostle will suffer it
The fact that both Clarke and Barnes send their readers by name to Lightfoot, whose annotation stands in the same catena

7.pericope_label: The argument from creation: the man is the image and glory of God and the woman the glory of the man, since she was made of him and for him; for which cause she ought to have power on her head, because of the angels

schools.summary: John Gill says that a man ought not to cover his head, and that the Ethiopic version adds the words whilst he prays, which is a proper interpretation though a wrong version, for the apostle's meaning is not that a man should not have his head covered at any time, but whilst he is in public worship, praying, prophesying or singing of psalms. John Calvin says that from the authority already established Paul draws an argument in favour of outward decorum: she is subject, says he, let her then wear a token of subjection; and in the term power there is an instance of metonymy, for he means a token by which she declares herself to be under the power of her husband, and it is a covering, whether a robe or a veil or any other kind of covering. It is asked whether he speaks of married women exclusively, Calvin says, for there are some that restrict what Paul here teaches to them, on the ground that it does not belong to virgins to be under the authority of a husband; it is however a mistake, for Paul looks beyond this to God's eternal law, which has made the female sex subject to the authority of men, and on this account all women are born that they may acknowledge themselves inferior in consequence of the superiority of the male sex. Otherwise it were an inconclusive argument that Paul has drawn from what is seemly, in saying that it were not one whit more becoming for a woman to be uncovered than to be shaven, Calvin says, this being applicable to virgins also. This passage about the angels is explained in various ways, Calvin says: as the Prophet Malachi calls priests angels, some are of opinion that Paul speaks of ministers, but the ministers of the word have nowhere that term applied to them by itself, that is, without something being added, and the meaning would be too forced; Calvin therefore understands it in its proper signification.

John Lightfoot says that what commonly obtains here is that by power is understood a veil, a sign of power above her, or of her subjection; but it is to be inquired whether to have power does not properly, yea always, denote to have power in one's own hand, and not a power above one, as in Matthew and John and elsewhere a thousand times. Because of the angels: because of what angels, Lightfoot asks, whether because of good angels, or because of bad, or because of the ministers? The reader knows what is said for this sense and for that and for the other, which Lightfoot will not repeat. Truly, he says, if he would understand a veil by the word power, then by angels he would understand devils, which are called angels in this very Epistle; and if he were of opinion that the apostle treated here of public assemblies only, he would render the words to the sense that a woman in the public assembly of the church ought to be covered.

Adam Clarke says there are few portions in the sacred writings that have given rise to such a variety of conjectures and explanations, and are less understood, than this verse; our translators were puzzled with it, and have inserted here one of the largest marginal readings found anywhere in their work, but this is only on the words power on her head, which they interpret as a covering, in sign that she is under the power of her husband, and, admitting this to be satisfactory so far as it goes, it by no means removes all the difficulty. Mr. Locke ingenuously acknowledged that he did not understand the meaning of the words, Clarke says, and almost every critic and learned man has a different explanation; some have endeavoured to force out a meaning by altering the text, and the emendation of Mr. Toup of Cornwall is the most remarkable, who reads a word meaning going out instead of the word power, so that the woman when she goes out should have a veil on her head; but whatever ingenuity there may appear in this emendation, the consideration that it is not acknowledged by any manuscript, or version, or primitive writer, is sufficient proof against it. Dr. Lightfoot, Schoettgen and Bishop Pearce have written best on the subject, Clarke says, and allow that there are many difficulties. Pearce contends that the original should be read, wherefore the woman ought to have a power upon her head, that is, the power of the husband over the wife, the word power standing for the sign or token of that power, which was a covering or veil; Theophylact explains the word as the symbol of being under power, that is, a veil or covering, and Photius explains it that to wear a veil on the head is a symbol of subjection, Clarke reports, and it is no unusual thing in the Old and New Testament for the signs and tokens of things to be called by the names of the things themselves, for thus circumcision is called the covenant though it was only the sign of it. The word angels presents another difficulty, Clarke says: some suppose that by these the apostle means the fallen angels, or devils, others the governors of the Church, and others those who were deputed among the Jews to espouse a virgin in the name of a lover; all these senses the learned bishop rejects, and believes that the apostle uses the word angels in its most obvious sense, for the heavenly angels, and that he speaks according to the notion which then prevailed among Jews, that the holy angels interested themselves in the affairs of men and particularly were present in their religious assemblies. Thus we read, neither say thou before the Angel, it was an error, Clarke says, and, I charge thee before God and the Lord Jesus Christ and the elect Angels; and parallel to these is what Agrippa says in his oration to the Jews in Josephus, I protest before God, your holy temple, and all the Angels of heaven; all which passages suppose, or were spoken to those who supposed, that the angels know what passes here upon earth. The notion, whether just or not, prevailed among the Jews, Clarke says, and if so St. Paul might speak according to the common opinion. Another difficulty lies in the phrase wherefore, which shows that this verse is a conclusion from what the apostle was arguing before, Clarke says, which we may understand thus, that his conclusion ought to have the more weight upon account of the presence, real or supposed, of the holy angels at their religious meetings. The learned bishop is not very willing to allow that the doctrine of the presence of angelic beings in religious assemblies is legitimate, Clarke says, but what difficulty can there be in this, if we take the words of the apostle in another place, are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation? And perhaps there is no time in which they can render more essential services to the followers of God than when they are engaged in divine ordinances. On the whole, Clarke reports the bishop's paraphrase thus: and because of this superiority in the man, I conclude that the woman should have on her head a veil, the mark of her husband's power over her, especially in the religious assemblies, where the angels are supposed to be invisibly present. The ancient versions make little alteration in the common reading, Clarke says, and the manuscripts leave the verse nearly as it stands in the common printed editions: the Armenian has a word that answers to a shade or covering, the Ethiopic reads that her head should be veiled, and the common editions of the Vulgate have power, but in an ancient edition of the Vulgate, perhaps one of the first ever printed, the verse stands, therefore the woman ought to have a covering upon her head, and because of the angels; Clarke's own old manuscript translation seems to have been taken from a manuscript which had the same reading, wherefore the woman schal haue a veyl on her heuyd, and for aungels, and some copies of the Itala have also a veil. In his view of this text Kypke differs from all others, Clarke says, and nothing that so judicious a critic advances should be lightly regarded: he contends that the word power occurs nowhere in the sense of veil, and yet supposes that the word veil is understood and must be supplied; he directs that a comma be placed after the word power and that it be construed with the verb ought, translating the verse, on this account the woman is subject to power, so that she should have a veil on her head, because of the angels; and he contends that both the Latins and Greeks use the verb to owe elegantly to express that to which one is obnoxious or liable, citing Horace, Dionysius of Halicarnassus and Euripides. Kypke contends that the words so taken agree perfectly with the context and with the wherefore in this verse, Clarke says: because the man was not created for the woman but the woman for the man, therefore she is subject to his authority and should have a veil on her head as a token of that subjection, and particularly before the holy angels who are present in the congregations of the saints. For Dr. Lightfoot's opinion, that by angels we are to understand the messengers who came on the part of others to look out for proper spouses for their friends, Clarke refers the reader to his works. The reader has now before him everything that is likely to cast light on this difficult subject, Clarke concludes, and he must either adopt what he judges to be best or else think for himself; after all, the custom of the Nazarite may cast some light upon this place, since a married woman was considered a Nazarite for life, that is, separated from all others and joined to one husband, who is her lord. John Wesley says that for this cause also a woman ought to be veiled in the public assemblies because of the angels, who attend there, and before whom they should be careful not to do anything indecent or irregular.

Charles Ellicott says that in the preceding verses the argument against the woman's head being uncovered was based upon the woman's relation to man and the man's relation to Christ in the Church, while in the three following verses the ground of the argument is changed and the same conclusion is arrived at from a review of the woman's relation to man and man's relation to God in the physical Creation. The external form of this argument is the same as that adopted previously, Ellicott says, the Apostle first stating what the man must not do and then conversely what the woman must do; he takes up the order of creation mentioned in Genesis, and the argument runs that man was made in the image of God and is the glory of God, but woman is the glory of the man, for woman was made out of man and man was not created for woman but woman as a help-meet for man; therefore man, as a created being, according to the accepted order of creation, is the direct representative of God, and woman the direct representative of man, and only indirectly and through him of God. The spiritual equality of man and wife does not upset this relationship, Ellicott says, and therefore an attempt to destroy the outward expression of it is to be condemned, as it would soon lead to an obliteration of the fact itself. It is to be remembered all through this passage, and it gives a further emphasis to the allusion to Adam and Eve, that St. Paul is only speaking of married women, Ellicott says: it is most unlikely that any case had occurred of an unmarried woman attempting such an outrage upon social feeling and national custom, and the Greek women when in public, except those of avowedly bad character, either wore a veil or drew the shawl over their heads. The two clauses which compose the tenth verse are perhaps the two most difficult passages in the New Testament, Ellicott says, and accordingly have given rise to an almost endless variety of interpretation. There have been many, some of them most fanciful, suggestions that the word for power may have crept in instead of some other word by the mistake of a copyist, or that the word used may have been one meaning when she goes out, or two words meaning in accordance with her nature; all explanations, however, which require an alteration in the Greek text must be set aside, Ellicott says, for there is no manuscript evidence whatever to support any other reading than the ordinary one, and any alteration of a difficult or unusual word would have been naturally into a word that would simplify the passage, whereas here, if alteration has taken place, it has been to insert a word which has increased the obscurity. It has been maintained that the word here means the sign of power, that is, a veil, which is the symbol of the husband's power over the wife, Ellicott says; the fatal objection to this view, however, is that the word expresses our own power and not the power exercised by another over us, being a word frequently used by St. Paul in that sense, so that whatever interpretation we put upon this passage it must be consistent with the word meaning some power which the woman herself has. Most commentators have quoted a passage from Diodorus Siculus in which the Greek word kingdom is used to signify a crown, as an illustration of the use of the word indicating the thing symbolised for the symbol itself, Ellicott says, and the parallelism between that and the use here has been very positively denied by Stanley and others, on the ground that the use of the name of the thing signified for the symbol, though natural when the power spoken of belongs to the person, would be unnatural when applied to the power exercised over that person by some one else; but the parallelism will hold good if we can refer the power here to some symbol of a power which belongs to the woman herself. If we bear in mind the Apostle's constant use of words with a double significance, and recall the reference to a woman's abundance of hair earlier and to her long hair later, where the hair given her by nature and the wearing of a veil are used as almost identical thoughts, we may conclude that the power here spoken of is that long hair which is called her glory, Ellicott says; it is remarkable that Callistratus twice uses this word in connection with hair to express its abundance, and to the Jews the recollection of Samson's history would have given the word power, when applied to hair, a remarkable significance. To thus turn aside abruptly in the middle of a long passage in which woman's subordination is enforced, and speak suddenly and vividly of her power, would be eminently Pauline, Ellicott says: in the Apostle's writings the thoughts of inferiority and superiority, of ruler and server, are frequently and almost paradoxically regarded as identical, and to serve because you rule, to be weak because you are in another sense strong, are thoughts strikingly combined again and again in his Epistles. Thus Ellicott would imagine him here to turn aside suddenly and say, I have been speaking of your subordination, and you are because of this to have a covering on your head as a sign, and yet that very thing which is the symbol of your subjection to man is the sign of your beauty and power as a woman. Why should a woman have her head covered because of the angels, Ellicott asks: the same objections already stated to any alteration of the text apply equally here, the manuscript evidence being unanimous in favour of the word angels, nor can we accept any of the figurative meanings attached to the word, as the president, or a messenger sent by enemies to see what took place, but must take the word in its ordinary and general sense. That the angels were present in assemblies for worship was an idea prevalent among the Jews, Ellicott says, and regarded as they were by the Christian as ministering spirits, no doubt their presence would be realised in the meetings of Christians. We have already seen that the Apostle in his argument upon the relation of the sexes refers to the first three chapters of Genesis, Ellicott says, and what more natural than that his thoughts should have gone on to the sixth of the same book, where is the record of the angels, in the Greek the word translated sons of God being angels, having been enamoured by the beauty of women and so having fallen from their high estate; this account is referred to more than once elsewhere in the New Testament and through Rabbinical interpretations would have been familiar to St. Paul's converts. Without at all necessarily expressing his belief in the historic accuracy of this legendary view of the fall of the angels, St. Paul might use it as an argument with those who did believe it, Ellicott says: you believe, would be his appeal to these women, that once, through seeing the beauty of the daughters of men, the holy angels themselves fell, and even that thought ought to make you feel that it is not seemly for you to be without a veil in those assemblies where the angels are present as God's ministering spirits. It has been urged by Meyer and others that the word angels in the New Testament always signifies good angels, Ellicott says, and it is in that sense he would regard it here, for the thought surely is that they are good angels and should not therefore be tempted, and he presumes the idea was also that the fallen angels were good before their fall. A.T. Robertson says the moral obligation rests on woman in the matter of dress that does not rest on the man, and that by the word power the apostle means a symbol of authority, but it is the sign of the authority of the man over the woman, the veil on the woman's head being the symbol of the authority that the man with the uncovered head has over her; it is, as we see it, more a sign of subjection than of authority. This startling phrase about the angels has caused all kinds of conjecture which may be dismissed, Robertson says: it is not preachers that Paul has in mind, nor evil angels who could be tempted, but angels present in worship who would be shocked at the conduct of the women, since the angels themselves veil their faces before Jehovah. Albert Barnes takes the argument from creation in the same order, that the man is the image and glory of God and the woman the glory of the man, and reads the covering as the appropriate emblem of the rank and station which God has assigned her.

debates: What the power on her head is: Ellicott and Lightfoot both argue from usage that the word always denotes a power one holds oneself and never a power held over one, Lightfoot saying so of a thousand places and Ellicott calling it the fatal objection to the common view; Ellicott then identifies the power with the woman's long hair, her glory, citing Callistratus and Samson, and finds the paradox eminently Pauline; Calvin, Clarke and Robertson take the word as metonymy for the token of another's authority, Clarke citing Theophylact and Photius, Robertson conceding that the veil is more a sign of subjection than of authority

Who the angels are: Wesley, Robertson and Clarke, the last following Pearce, take them for the holy angels present in worship, Robertson adding that they themselves veil their faces before Jehovah and Clarke supporting the Jewish notion from Ecclesiastes, from the charge before the elect angels, and from Agrippa's oration in Josephus; Calvin knows and rejects the view that ministers are meant, since Malachi calls priests angels, as too forced; Lightfoot says that if the power is a veil then the angels are devils, who are so called in this same epistle; Ellicott refers the phrase to the fall of the angels in Genesis, used as an argument with those who believed the story, and against Meyer keeps them good angels who should not be tempted

Whether the passage concerns married women only: Ellicott restricts it to them throughout, thinking it most unlikely that an unmarried woman had attempted such an outrage on custom; Calvin expressly denies the restriction, holding that Paul looks beyond marriage to God's eternal law, and arguing that the appeal to what is seemly would otherwise fail, since it is no more becoming for a virgin to be shaven than for a wife

Whether the text may be emended: Clarke reports Toup of Cornwall's change of a single word to give when she goes out, and rejects it because no manuscript, version or primitive writer supports it; Ellicott sets aside that whole class of conjecture on the principle that alteration of a difficult word would naturally have simplified it, whereas these increase the obscurity; Kypke, reported by Clarke, leaves the text alone but repoints the construction so that the woman is subject to power
outliers: Ellicott's judgement that the two clauses of this verse are perhaps the two most difficult passages in the New Testament

Clarke's report that our translators were so puzzled that they inserted one of the largest marginal readings found anywhere in their work, and that Locke ingenuously acknowledged he did not understand the words

Clarke's citation of an early printed Vulgate reading simply that the woman ought to have a covering upon her head, and because of the angels, matched by his own old manuscript English, that she schal haue a veyl on her heuyd, and for aungels
Ellicott's observation that to serve because you rule, and to be weak because you are in another sense strong, are thoughts strikingly combined again and again in Paul
Clarke's closing refusal to decide, handing the question to the reader to adopt what he judges best or else think for himself
Clarke's final suggestion that the custom of the Nazarite may cast light here, a married woman being a Nazarite for life, separated from all others and joined to one husband

11.pericope_label: The corrective that neither is without the other in the Lord, the appeal to their own judgement and to nature, the glory of a woman long hair and the shame of it in a man, and the closing appeal to the custom of the churches

schools.summary: John Gill takes the words neither is the man without the woman, nor the woman without the man, in the Lord, to mean that in the Lord, that is in the Christian economy and in the church state, the one is not without the other, but each is necessary to the other, so that the subordination just laid down is not to be pressed into a separation. Gill takes the hair given for a covering in its plain sense, as an ornament bestowed by the Author of nature, and reads the appeal to the churches at the close as an appeal to a settled and universal practice, from which the Corinthians had no warrant to depart. John Calvin says that Paul, having spoken of the subjection of the woman, now adds a corrective, lest men should abuse their authority: the man cannot do without the woman, nor the woman without the man, and this is said in the Lord, that is, according to the appointment of God in the Christian order, so that the mutual obligation of the sexes is not overthrown by the difference of rank between them. Calvin traces the argument to its source in God, since the woman was of the man at the first and the man is by the woman ever since, but all things are of God, so that neither sex has ground of boasting against the other, the whole order being God's arrangement and not their own. On the last verse Calvin holds that Paul, having reasoned at length, at last cuts off further dispute by an appeal to the practice of the churches, since a contentious spirit is not to be satisfied by argument, and the consent of the churches of God is a sufficient answer to a wrangler.

John Lightfoot, on the words her hair is given her for a covering, brings in a rabbinic story of the daughter of Nicodemus, who being reduced to miserable poverty went to the Rabbi, and he sets the Talmudic material on the hair and covering of women beside the apostle's argument, as he has done throughout the chapter. His annotations here belong to the same Horae Hebraicae from which both Clarke and Barnes have already quoted him by name, and they turn on the Jewish understanding of a woman's hair as at once her ornament and, in certain circumstances, the token of her shame.

Adam Clarke says nature certainly teaches us, by bestowing it, that it is proper for women to have long hair, and that it is not so with men: the hair of the male rarely grows like that of a female unless art is used, and even then it bears but a scanty proportion to the former, hence it is truly womanish to have long hair and it is a shame to the man who affects it. In ancient times the people of Achaia, the province in which Corinth stood, and the Greeks in general were noted for their long hair, Clarke says, and hence they are called by Homer, in a great variety of places, the long-haired Achaeans; soldiers in different countries have been distinguished for their long hair, but whether this can be said to their praise or blame, or whether Homer uses it always as a term of respect when he applies it to the Greeks, Clarke will not wait to inquire. Long hair was certainly not in repute among the Jews, Clarke says: the Nazarites let their hair grow, but it was as a token of humiliation, and it is possible that St. Paul had this in view, so that there were two reasons why the apostle should condemn this practice, first because it was a sign of humiliation and secondly because it was womanish. After all it is possible that St. Paul may refer to dressed, frizzled and curled hair, which shallow and effeminate men might have affected in that time as they do in this, Clarke says; perhaps there is not a sight more ridiculous in the eye of common sense than a high-dressed, curled, cued and powdered head, with which the operator must have taken considerable pains and the silly patient lost much time and comfort in submitting to what all but senseless custom must call an indignity and degradation; hear nature, common sense and reason, and they will inform you that if a man have long hair it is a shame unto him. The Author of their being has given a larger proportion of hair to the head of women than to that of men, Clarke says, and to them it is an especial ornament and may in various cases serve as a veil; it is a certain fact that a man's long hair renders him contemptible and a woman's long hair renders her more amiable, and nature and the apostle speak the same language, however we may account for it. If any person sets himself up as a wrangler, putting himself forward as a defender of such points, that a woman may pray or teach with her head uncovered and that a man may without reproach have long hair, let him know that we have no such custom as either, nor are they sanctioned by any of the Churches of God, whether among the Jews or the Gentiles, Clarke says; and we have already seen that the verb which we translate to seem generally strengthens and increases the sense. From the attention that the apostle has paid to the subject of veils and hair, Clarke concludes, it is evident that it must have occasioned considerable disturbance in the Church of Corinth, and they have produced evil effects in much later times. John Wesley takes the eleventh and twelfth verses as a mutual limitation, that in the Lord Jesus there is neither male nor female in respect of the blessings of the gospel, and that as the woman was at first taken out of the man, so the man is ever since born of the woman, but all things are of God, who is the original of all. Wesley reads the appeal to nature as an appeal to what universal custom and the common sense of mankind agree in, and takes the hair given for a covering to mean that nature herself has taught the woman what she ought to wear; on the last verse he says that if any man be contentious and disposed to dispute the point, the apostle cuts him short by saying that neither the apostles nor the churches of God have any such custom.

Charles Ellicott says that here follow words of caution, lest the previous express declaration of the subordination of woman to man might be exaggerated or perverted: this very subordination of one sex to the other implies a mutual connection and not an isolation of each sex, and the woman is not independent of but dependent on the man in the Lord, that is, in the Christian economy.
