An appeal to the original act of creation proves the truth of the previous statement of the interdependence of the sexes, Ellicott says: if already the fact of woman's having been taken out of man was used as an argument to prove her subordination, there is now coupled with that fact of the origin of woman that other fact of the perpetual birth of man from woman, to show that there is a mutual relation; the first woman was made out of man, therefore woman is dependent on man, and every man has been born of a woman, therefore man is not independent of woman. In the Greek the word rendered of represents a finite act and the word rendered by a continued process, Ellicott notes; and thus, as usual, St. Paul completes the thought by tracing all up to God, for the mediate processes of their origin may differ but the source of their being is common, since they, and all beings, and all things, and the sequence of all things come of God. In the following verses the Apostle reasons with them, appeals to their own common sense and to the indications of Nature as to the evident truth of what he has taught them, Ellicott says: surely you would not think it seemly for a woman, setting aside the question of men and angels altogether, to speak face to face with God in prayer? Nature itself may mean either the native inborn sense of what is seemly, as contrasted with revelation, or it may signify the ordinary and evident arrangement of things in creation, Ellicott says, and probably the former is the true meaning, referring to the fact that the heathen who had no direct revelation did by nature, in regarding long hair as a woman's glory, the things contained in the Law. We should follow the suggestions of Nature, Ellicott says: if a woman has naturally long hair, which is given to her as a covering for her head, the covering of her head can be no shame to her, therefore let her wear a veil, for the will ought to correspond to Nature. The argument and the appeal to their own good sense having been completed, the Apostle now adds that if after all some one continues to argue the matter captiously and is not satisfied with the reason given, the answer to such a one must be simply that we, the Apostles and the churches of God, have no such custom as that women should pray and teach with uncovered head, Ellicott says. It has been suggested that the word custom refers not to the uncovering of the head but to the contention just mentioned, Ellicott notes, but the former interpretation seems more natural, and the Apostle's object here is not so much merely to censure the contentious spirit as to show how such an objector must be dealt with. It is noticeable that the appeal is made to the practice of the churches in the plural and not the Church, Ellicott says: thus it is not the authority of the Church as such that is quoted, but it is the uniformity of practice in the several Christian churches that is appealed to, and the Church in Corinth has no right to become exceptional. Ellicott makes two general remarks on the scope and bearing of this remarkable passage. As St. Paul taught regarding slavery that the object of Christianity was not to suddenly efface existing political arrangements, so he teaches here that Christianity did not seek to obliterate those social distinctions which were universally recognised, Ellicott says: we know now how mighty an instrument Christ's religion has been in elevating the social condition of woman, but this has been accomplished by gradually leavening the world with Christian principle and not by sudden external revolution. The arguments and illustrations which the Apostle here employs have a more abiding and a wider application than the particular case to which he applied them, Ellicott says, and the lesson which they teach us is that Christianity did not come to unsex woman, but to raise, dignify and ennoble her as woman, to abolish for ever her real wrongs but not to yield to a revolutionary clamour for imaginary rights; Old and New Testament alike emphasise the truth that, as has been quaintly and truly said, woman was not made from man's head to be his ruler, nor from his feet to be his slave, but from his side to be his equal, and from beneath his strong arm to demand his protection. Secondly, the influence of St. Paul's instruction as to women not uncovering their heads in public worship has lasted long after the necessity for that particular expression of her relationship to man has passed away, Ellicott says: while in succeeding ages again and again some have forgotten the principles of the teaching, which are eternal, the particular application of them, which was only temporary, has been continuously and universally observed. Surely this is an illustration and evidence of the divine wisdom which withheld the apostolic writers from, as a rule, laying down minute directions for worship or dogmatic formulas of faith, Ellicott says, for men would, in a servile obedience to rules, have soon and completely forgotten the living principles on which they were based; and to this day the universal custom in Christian places of worship of women being covered and men uncovered, together with the increasing revolt against the acknowledgment of the subordination of woman to man of which that practice was originally the avowed symbol, is a striking proof of how the same spirit which led Jews of old to be scrupulous in their observance of certain external ordinances, while forgetting the weightier matters of which they were to be the outward expression, was not merely a Jewish but a human weakness. A.T. Robertson says the Apostle reinforces the appeal to custom by the appeal to nature in a question that expects the affirmative answer, and that the word for nature, from an old verb meaning to produce, is difficult to define: here it means native sense of propriety, in addition to mere custom, but one that rests on the objective difference in the constitution of things. Long hair is a glory to a woman and a disgrace to a man, as we still feel, Robertson says, and there is a papyrus example of a priest accused of letting his hair grow long and of wearing woollen garments; the word rendered for a covering is an old word meaning something flung around, as a mantle or a veil, and the hair is not in the place of a veil but answers to one, as a permanent endowment. The word rendered contentious is an old adjective meaning fond of strife, occurring only here in the New Testament, Robertson says, so that if the disputatious brother only existed in this instance, so much the better; and the word rendered custom means intercourse or intimacy, occurring in the New Testament only here and earlier in this epistle, while Vincent notes that in the sculptures of the catacombs the women have a close-fitting head-dress, while the men have the hair short. Albert Barnes says the design of these verses is to guard the woman from being depressed by what has gone before, and to show that in the plan of salvation the sexes are in many respects on an equality, the same plan being adapted to both, the same blessings appointed for both and the same high hopes held out to both.

debates: What the custom disowned in the last verse is: Ellicott reports the suggestion that it refers to the contentiousness just mentioned and prefers the uncovering, since the Apostle's object is to show how the objector must be dealt with; Clarke takes it as covering both faults at once, the woman's bare head and the man's long hair, sanctioned by no church of God whether among Jews or Gentiles; Calvin and Wesley read the verse as a deliberate refusal to argue further with a wrangler, the consent of the churches being answer enough

What nature means in the appeal: Ellicott offers the native inborn sense of what is seemly as against the arrangement of things in creation, and prefers the former, comparing the heathen who without revelation do by nature the things of the law; Robertson takes both together, a native sense of propriety in addition to custom but resting on the objective difference in the constitution of things; Clarke argues it as plain biology, that the male's hair rarely grows like the female's unless art is used

How far the corrective in the eleventh and twelfth verses reaches: Ellicott makes it a caution against exaggerating the subordination, since subordination implies mutual connection and not isolation; Barnes makes it a comfort, designed to keep the woman from being depressed by what precedes and to show the sexes on an equality in the plan of salvation; Calvin and Gill anchor it in the phrase in the Lord, taking the mutual dependence as holding within the Christian order

Whether the appeal at the close is to authority or to practice: Ellicott presses that the plural churches is used and not the Church, so that what is quoted is uniformity of usage rather than institutional authority, and that Corinth has no right to become exceptional; Clarke and Wesley treat the same clause as simply closing the argument against a wrangler
outliers: Ellicott's judgement that Christianity did not come to unsex woman but to raise and ennoble her as woman, abolishing her real wrongs without yielding to a clamour for imaginary rights
The saying Ellicott quotes as quaint and true, that woman was made not from man's head to be his ruler nor from his feet to be his slave, but from his side to be his equal

Ellicott's second moral, that the temporary application of this rule has been universally kept while the eternal principle behind it has been forgotten, which he takes as evidence of the wisdom that withheld the apostles from laying down minute directions for worship
Clarke's tirade against the high-dressed, curled and powdered head, over which the operator takes considerable pains and the silly patient loses much time and comfort
Clarke's citation of Homer's long-haired Achaeans, the Greeks of the very province in which Corinth stood

Robertson's papyrus of a priest accused of letting his hair grow long and wearing woollen garments, and Vincent's note that in the catacomb sculptures the women wear a close-fitting head-dress and the men short hair
Robertson's dry wish that the disputatious brother existed only in this instance

17.pericope_label: Paul turns from the veil to the assembly itself, praising them not, since they come together not for the better but for the worse; there are divisions among them, and there must be heresies also, that the approved may be made manifest

schools.summary: John Gill takes the divisions to be the same old factions reported at the beginning of the epistle, now showing themselves in the very assembly where the Supper was eaten; the apostle says he partly believes the report, not giving credit to every part of it, yet not able to disbelieve it altogether, since it came from persons of credit in the house of Chloe. Gill says the heresies are not to be understood of doctrinal errors only, but of the parties and sects into which the divisions hardened, and that God in his providence suffers such things to be, that those who are approved of him, being tried and found faithful, may be made manifest to others. John Calvin says the apostle had previously spoken of schisms and now uses the term heresies with the view of amplifying the more, as we may infer from the word also, which is added for the sake of amplification. It is well known in what sense the ancients used those two terms, and what distinction they made between heretics and schismatics, Calvin says: they made heresy to consist in disagreement as to doctrine, and schism, on the contrary, in alienation of affection, as when any one withdrew from the Church from envy, or from dislike of the pastors, or from ill nature. It is true that the Church cannot but be torn asunder by false doctrine, and thus heresy is the root and origin of schism, and it is also true that envy or pride is the mother of almost all heresies, Calvin says, but at the same time it is of advantage to distinguish in this way between these two terms. Calvin has already expressed his disapprobation of those who explain heresy as meaning the setting up of a separate table, inasmuch as the rich did not partake of their Supper along with the poor, for the apostle had it in view to point out something more hateful. Without mentioning the opinions of others, Calvin takes schism and heresy here in the way of less and greater: schisms are either secret grudges, when we do not see that agreement which ought to subsist among the pious, when inclinations at variance with each other are at work, when every one is mightily pleased with his own way and finds fault with everything that is done by others; heresies are when the evil proceeds to such a pitch that open hostility is discovered, and persons deliberately divide themselves into opposite parties. Hence, in order that believers might not feel discouraged on seeing the Corinthians torn with divisions, the Apostle turns round this occasion of offence in an opposite direction, intimating that the Lord does rather by such trials make proof of his people's constancy, Calvin says: a lovely consolation. So far should we be from being troubled or cast down when we do not see complete unity in the Church, but on the contrary some threatenings of separation from want of proper agreement, that even if sects should start up on all sides we ought to remain firm and constant, Calvin says; for in this way hypocrites are detected, and in this way, on the other hand, the sincerity of believers is tried, since this gives occasion for discovering the fickleness of those who were not rooted in the Lord's Word, and the wickedness of those who had assumed the appearance of good men, while the good afford a more signal manifestation of their constancy and sincerity. But observe what Paul says, Calvin adds, for he intimates by the expression that this state of matters does not happen by chance but by the sure providence of God, because he has it in view to try his people as gold in the furnace, and if it is agreeable to the mind of God it is consequently expedient. At the same time, however, we must not enter into thorny disputes, or rather into labyrinths, as to a fatal necessity, Calvin warns: we know that there never will be a time when there will not be many reprobates, that they are governed by the spirit of Satan and are effectually drawn away to what is evil, and that Satan in his activity leaves no stone unturned with the view of breaking up the unity of the Church; from this, and not from fate, comes that necessity of which Paul makes mention.

Matthew Henry says that the apostle, having reproved the disorder about the veil, now comes to a much greater fault, and one that touched the very ordinance of the Lord's Supper: he could not praise them in this, for their assemblies were so managed that they came together not for the better but for the worse, and the very meetings which should have edified them did them harm. Henry observes that when the ordinances of God are so corrupted in the administration that the people are the worse and not the better for attending them, the fault is a heavy one, and that the divisions among the Corinthians, already reproved at the opening of the epistle, had now made their way into the most solemn act of Christian worship. He notes further that the apostle believed the report in part, which shows both that he was not credulous of every evil rumour and that he had good ground for what he did believe; and that the permission of parties in the church is turned by God to a good end, since the trial makes the sound and the unsound alike apparent, so that the approved are made manifest.

Adam Clarke says that in the beginning of this epistle the apostle did praise them for their attention in general to the rules he had laid down, but here he is obliged to condemn certain irregularities which had crept in among them, particularly relative to the celebration of the Lord's Supper. Through some false teaching which they had received in the absence of the apostle, they appear to have celebrated it precisely in the same way the Jews did their passover, Clarke says: that, we know, was a regular meal, only accompanied with certain peculiar circumstances and ceremonies, two of which were eating bread solemnly broken and drinking a cup of wine called the cup of blessing; now it is certain that our Lord has taken these two things and made them expressive of the crucifixion of his body and the shedding of his blood, as an atonement for the sins of mankind. The teachers which had crept into the Corinthian Church appear to have perverted the whole of this divine institution, Clarke says, for the celebration of the Lord's Supper appears to have been made among them a part of an ordinary meal: the people came together and it appears brought their provisions with them, some had much and others had less, some ate to excess and others had scarcely enough to suffice nature, one was hungry and the other was drunken, that is, filled to the full, which is the sense of the word in many places of Scripture. At the conclusion of this irregular meal they appear to have done something in reference to our Lord's institution, but more resembling the Jewish passover, Clarke says; these irregularities, connected with so many indecencies, the apostle reproves, for instead of being benefited by the divine ordinance they were injured, and came together not for the better but for the worse. There be divisions among you, that is, they had schisms among them, Clarke says: the old parties were kept up, even in the place where they assembled to eat the Lord's Supper, and the Paulians, the Kephites and the Apollonians continued to be distinct parties, and ate their meals separately, even in the same house. There must be also heresies, Clarke says, meaning not a common consent of the members of the Church, either in the doctrines of the Gospel or in the ceremonies of the Christian religion: their difference in religious opinion led to a difference in their religious practice, and thus the Church of God, that should have been one body, was split into sects and parties, the divisions and the heresies springing out of each other; and Clarke refers the reader to his larger note on the word heresy in the Acts. John Wesley says that the apostle does not praise them in this, that they come together not for the better but for the worse, their very assemblies being hurtful to them; that the divisions are the parties and contentions already spoken of, which showed themselves even at the Lord's table; and that there must be heresies, or opinions causing divisions, among them, that those who are approved, being tried and found faithful, may be made manifest, God overruling even these evils to a good end.

Charles Ellicott renders the opening better as, now I give you this command, while not praising you that you come together not for the better but for the worse, and says these words lead from the subject which has gone before to another and different abuse of liberty in public assemblies. There were evidently three great abuses which had crept into the Church, Ellicott says: the discarding by the women of the covering for their heads, which concerned one sex only and has been treated of already; the disorders at the Lord's Supper; and the misuse of spiritual gifts, the former of these two occupying the remainder of this chapter while the latter is discussed in the next. To render the Greek word as I declare and so make it refer to what is about to follow gives a more logical completeness to the passage, Ellicott says, but is scarcely allowable, since the word elsewhere always means a distinct command; others have suggested that St. Paul anticipates in thought the practical direction which occurs at the end of the chapter, but this view is open to the objections that it completely isolates this verse from the one before it, while the Greek evidently intimates a connection, and that it is unnatural to separate the statement so far from the command to which it refers. It is better to regard these words as forming a sort of intellectual isthmus connecting the two wide fields of thought which the earlier and later portions of the chapter embrace, Ellicott says. I praise you not carries the thought back to the second verse, and shows that the commendation expressed there is still the writer's starting-point, or rather the point of departure from which he proceeds to censure, Ellicott says; and the passage is not, I do not praise you because you come together, but, I do not praise your coming together not for the better but for the worse. We in vain look for the secondly which in a perfectly systematic treatise should follow this first of all, Ellicott says: some writers maintain that the eighteenth and nineteenth verses form the first point and the rest the second, but there is no indication of a new subject being introduced, the repetition of the words come together carrying the mind back at once to the earlier come together. It is better to consider the first point to be the abuse regarding the Lord's Supper, which is more immediately treated of, and the second point the abuse of spiritual gifts commencing with the next chapter, Ellicott says: they are two branches of the one general subject, irregularities in religious assemblies, and although the latter is not connected with the former by a definite secondly, there is a sufficient verbal indication that a second topic is entered upon. It is well to remember in this and similar cases that this is not a treatise but a letter, Ellicott says, and not only a letter but an answer to a letter, and that if we had a copy of the epistle to which this is a reply, many points of sequence and arrangement which at present present difficulties would be as clear to us as they were to those who originally received this Epistle. When ye come together in the church refers not to a locality but to the character of the assembly, as we should say in church, or in parliament, Ellicott says: the spirit of faction which has already been dealt with as pervading Christian society had invaded the Christian assemblies. The words I partly believe it are full of the courtesy and charity so characteristic of the Apostle, Ellicott says, and they suggest to us all a lesson regarding our belief of evil reports, even when reaching us on the very best authority, for the general practice is to believe a little more than we are told, whereas St. Paul believed a part only of what he was told. For there must be also heresies is better rendered, for there must be also sects, Ellicott says, and there have been many attempts to explain where lies the difference between the divisions of the former verse and the sects of this one; from all that we know of the Apostolic Church it is clear that neither of these words can mean sects separated from the Church, but parties in the Church. Christ had foretold that stumbling-blocks or scandals must arise in the Church, Ellicott says, and it is possible that our Lord on some occasion spoke of these as sects, since Justin Martyr attributes the use of this very word to our Lord, and St. Paul possibly uses the word here because it was the one traditionally reported as having been used by Christ in some of his unrecorded utterances. Christ has foretold that in the divine economy of permission such divisions will arise, Ellicott says: they are allowed because this is a state of continual judgment, and the existence of such offences will be God's means of manifesting those who are void of offence and those who are not. A.T. Robertson says there is no antithesis expressed to the first of all, no secondly or in the next place, this being the primary reason for Paul's condemnation and the only one given; that here the word church has the literal meaning of assembly; that the word for divisions is an old word for cleft or rent, with an example in the papyri for a splinter of wood, and denotes not yet formal cleavages into two or more organizations but partisan divisions that showed in the love-feasts and at the Lord's Supper; and that the rumours of strife were so constant that the apostle keeps on hearing them. Since moral conditions are so bad among them there must be heresies, Robertson says, the schisms naturally becoming factions or parties: heresy is theoretical schism, and schism practical heresy. God's purpose in these factions makes the proved ones become manifest, Robertson says, quoting Findlay that these parties are a magnet attracting unsound and unsettled minds, and adding that it has always been so, with instances from the movements of his own day. Albert Barnes says the apostle proceeds to notice an abuse in regard to the Lord's Supper which had prevailed among them, and that he could not commend them in this; the divisions were the party strifes already reproved, which had followed them even to the table of the Lord, and the heresies are the parties or sects thence arising, permitted by God in order that those who are approved, and who hold fast the truth amidst the prevailing errors, may be made manifest to all.

John Chrysostom says it is necessary in considering the present charge to state also first the occasion of it, for thus again will our discourse be more intelligible. As in the case of the three thousand who believed in the beginning, all had eaten their meals in common and had all things common, such also was the practice at the time when the Apostle wrote this, Chrysostom says: not such indeed exactly, but as it were a certain outflowing of that communion which abode among them descended also to them that came after. Because of course some were poor but others rich, they laid not down all their goods in the midst, but made the tables open on stated days, as it should seem, Chrysostom says; and when the solemn service was completed, after the communion of the Mysteries, they all went to a common entertainment, the rich bringing their provisions with them, and the poor and destitute being invited by them, and all feasting in common. But afterward this custom also became corrupt, Chrysostom says, and the reason was their being divided and addicting themselves, some to this party and others to that, and saying, I am of such a one, and I of such a one; which thing also to correct the apostle said at the beginning of the Epistle that it had been signified to him concerning them, by them which are of the household of Chloe, that there were contentions among them, and that each one of them said, I am of Paul, and I of Apollos, and I of Cephas. Not that Paul was the person to whom they were attaching themselves, Chrysostom says, for he would not have borne it, but wishing by concession to tear up this custom from the root he introduced himself, indicating that if any one had inscribed upon himself even his name when breaking off from the common body, even so the thing done was profane and extreme wickedness; and if in his case it were wickedness, much more in the case of those who were inferior to him.

debates: How the abuse at the Supper arose: Chrysostom describes a decay from within, the common meal of the first believers surviving as an open table on stated days after the communion of the Mysteries, until the party spirit corrupted it; Clarke ascribes it instead to false teachers who in Paul's absence made them keep the Supper as the Jews kept the passover, so that the divine institution became part of an ordinary meal with the sacrament appended at the end

What separates divisions from heresies: Calvin reports the ancient distinction, heresy in doctrine and schism in affection, but takes the words here as less and greater, schisms being secret grudges and heresies open hostility with deliberate parties; Robertson compresses it to the epigram that heresy is theoretical schism and schism practical heresy; Ellicott insists neither can mean bodies separated from the Church but only parties within it, and suggests Paul may be quoting a word of Christ himself, since Justin Martyr attributes it to him; Clarke makes the difference practical, that difference of opinion led to difference of practice

Where the answering second point is: Robertson observes flatly that no antithesis to the first of all is expressed and that this is the only reason given; Ellicott canvasses the proposals and settles that the first point is the disorder at the Supper and the second the abuse of spiritual gifts in the following chapter, and turns the difficulty into a caution, that this is a letter answering a letter, so that much which puzzles us was plain to those who first received it

Why God permits the parties: Calvin makes it a trial of constancy and calls it a lovely consolation, while refusing the labyrinth of a fatal necessity, since the necessity comes from the reprobates whom Satan governs and not from fate; Barnes, Gill and Wesley take it simply as the means by which the approved are made manifest; Robertson adds Findlay's image of such parties as a magnet for unsound and unsettled minds
outliers: Ellicott's lesson from the words I partly believe it, that the general practice is to believe a little more than we are told, whereas St. Paul believed only a part of what he was told
Ellicott's reminder that this is not a treatise but a letter, and an answer to a letter, so that if we had the letter it replies to, many difficulties of arrangement would vanish
Ellicott's description of the seventeenth verse as an intellectual isthmus joining the two wide fields of thought in this chapter
Clarke's picture of the Paulians, the Kephites and the Apollonians eating their meals separately even in the same house
Chrysostom's report that Paul put his own name at the head of the party list by concession, in order to tear the custom up by the root
Calvin's refusal to be drawn into labyrinths about a fatal necessity, locating the necessity in Satan's activity rather than in fate
Robertson's citation of the papyri for the word rendered divisions, used there of a splinter of wood

20.pericope_label: Their assembling is not to eat the Lord’s supper, since each takes his own supper first, one being hungry while another is drunken; have they not houses to eat in, or do they despise the church of God and shame those that have not?

schools.summary: John Gill says that when they came together into one place it was not to eat the Lord's supper, that is, their end and design was not this, nor could their behaviour be so called; and that the apostle's meaning is that the ordinance was so shamefully abused that it lost the name, being turned into a common meal. Gill notes that they should have eaten their ordinary food in their own houses, and that the poor were put to shame by the disparity of the tables. John Calvin says the apostle now reproves the abuse that had crept in among the Corinthians as to the Lord's Supper, in respect of their mixing up profane banquets with the sacred and spiritual feast, and that too with contempt of the poor. Paul says that in this way it is not the Lord's Supper that is partaken of, Calvin explains: not that a single abuse altogether set aside the sacred institution of Christ and reduced it to nothing, but that they polluted the sacrament by observing it in a wrong way, for we are accustomed to say in common conversation that a thing is not done at all if it is not done aright. If you understand the words as meaning that it is not lawful, as some take them, the meaning will amount to the same thing, Calvin says, that the Corinthians were not in a state of preparation for partaking of the supper, being in so divided a state; but what he has stated is more simple, that the apostle condemns that profane admixture which had nothing in it akin to the Lord's Supper. It is truly wonderful, and next to a miracle, that Satan could have accomplished so much in so short a time, Calvin says: we are admonished by this instance how much antiquity, without reason on its side, can effect, or in other words how much influence a long continued custom has while not sanctioned by a single declaration of the word of God, for this, having become customary, was looked upon as lawful. Paul was then at hand to interfere, Calvin says; what then must have been the state of matters after the death of the Apostles, and with what liberty must Satan have sported himself? Yet here is the great strength of Papists, that the thing is ancient, it was done long ago, let it therefore have the weight of a revelation from heaven. It is uncertain, however, what was the origin of this abuse, or what was the occasion of its springing up so soon, Calvin says: Chrysostom is of opinion that it originated in the love-feasts, and that while the rich had been accustomed at first to bring with them from their houses the means of feasting with the poor indiscriminately and in common, they afterwards began to exclude the poor and to guzzle over their delicacies by themselves; and certainly it appears from Tertullian that that custom was a very ancient one. Pliny is supposed to refer to the love-feasts in his letter to Trajan, Calvin notes, where he says of the Christians in Bithynia, of which he was governor, that upon examination they affirmed that it was customary for them to depart and come together again for the purpose of taking an innocent repast in common; and they gave the name of loves to those common entertainments which they contrived among themselves, as being tokens of fraternal affection, consisting of alms. Nor has Calvin any doubt that it took its rise from sacrificial rites commonly observed both by Jews and Gentiles, for he observes that Christians for the most part corrected the faults connected with those rites in such a manner as to retain at the same time some resemblance; hence it is probable that, on observing that both Jews and Gentiles added a feast to their sacrifice as an appendage to it, but that both of them sinned in respect of ambition, luxury and intemperance, they instituted in process of time a kind of banquet which might accustom them rather to sobriety and frugality, and might at the same time be in accordance with a spiritual entertainment in respect of mutual fellowship, for in it the poor were entertained at the expense of the rich and the table was open to all. But whether they had from the very first fallen into this profane abuse, or whether an institution otherwise not so objectionable had in this way degenerated in process of time, Paul would have them in no way mix up this spiritual banquet with common feasts, Calvin says: this indeed looks well, that the poor along with the rich partake in common of the provisions that have been brought, and that the rich share of their abundance along with the needy, but nothing ought to have such weight with us as to lead us to profane the holy sacrament.

John Lightfoot says he wonders that the Agape, the love feasts of which St. Jude speaks, should among interpreters receive their exposition from this place. He quotes Beza, who says that in those feasts which they call Agape they used to take the holy supper of the Lord, as appears from this chapter, and of which thing discourse is had in Tertullian's Apologetic and in other writings of the ancients; and Beza again, that the apostle passes here to another head of his discourse, namely the administration of the Lord's supper, to which the love feasts were joined, and that although the love feasts had been used a long while in the church and commendably too, the apostles themselves being the authors of them, yet the apostle judges them to be taken away because of their abuse. Lightfoot also quotes Baronius to the same effect, that the use of a most commendable thing continued as yet in the church, that as Christ had done at his last supper and had admonished his disciples to do in remembrance of him, Christians meeting in the church should sup together and withal should receive the most holy eucharist.

Adam Clarke says that every one took his own supper before: they had a grand feast, though the different sects kept in parties by themselves, but all took as ample a supper as they could provide, each bringing his own provisions with him, before they took what was called the Lord's Supper. They should have taken their ordinary meal at home and have come together in the church to celebrate the Lord's Supper, Clarke says; and by despising the church of God they rendered the sacred assembly and the place contemptible by their conduct, showing themselves destitute of that respect which they owed to the place set apart for divine worship. Them that have not means them that are poor, Clarke says, not them who had not victuals at that time, but those who are so poor as to be incapable of furnishing themselves as others had done. John Wesley says that when they came together into one place it was not to eat the Lord's supper, for that was not the design nor the effect of their meeting; that every one took his own supper before, the rich eating what they had brought and leaving the poor unprovided, so that one was hungry and another drunken; and that they had houses to eat and drink in, so that the church was not the place for a common meal, and by making it so they despised the church of God and put the poor to shame.

Charles Ellicott renders the verse better as, therefore, when you assemble in the same place, it is not to eat the supper dedicated to the Lord, and says that, regarding the previous verse as a parenthesis, the word therefore connects this with the eighteenth: there being divisions among them, it is not possible for them when they assemble as a Church body to partake of that supper which is dedicated to the Lord. The whole meal, or charity-feast, was distinguished from other meals by being united with the Lord's Supper, Ellicott says: to these charity-feasts the Christians brought contributions of food, the rich of their abundance and the poor whatever they could afford, and the food thus provided was partaken of in common by all; the Greek words in this verse for Lord's Supper are more general than those used later in the chapter, the whole meal being dedicated to the Lord by virtue of its union with the sacramental Supper. Here follows a description of the conduct at this feast which renders it impossible for it to be a Lord's Supper, Ellicott says: every one greedily seizes, that is, takes before distribution is made, what he has brought with him, and appropriates it to his own individual use instead of making it a contribution to the general supply, so that every one comes to eat his own supper and not the Lord's Supper, and the result is that while some poor man who has not been able to bring enough for himself remains unfed, some rich man, drinking the wine which he brought and has not shared, is drunken. The next verse is better rendered, surely it is not that you have no houses to eat and drink in, Ellicott says: this cannot be the explanation of their conduct, for they have houses in which they can enjoy their proper meals, so that hunger and thirst, which can be satisfied at home, cannot be the explanation of their conduct at the charity-feasts. The only other alternative explanation, therefore, is that they despise an assembly which is the Church of God, Ellicott says, and put to shame those poor members, who no doubt were the majority, who have not houses in which to eat and drink and have come together in this common assembly to share in the food which the wealthier members ought to contribute. The shame which a poor man will feel when the rich come to these feasts bringing supplies for their own private use and not for general distribution will arise both from the striking contrast, which will come out all the more vividly from his poverty being brought into such direct contact with the wealth of the rich, and from the evident dislike of the rich to partake of a common meal with the poor, Ellicott says; thus those assemblies will, through the misconduct of the wealthier Christians, have precisely the opposite result from that which they were intended to accomplish, being an assembly in one place but not to partake of one supper. The Apostle asks indignantly whether such conduct can be included in the catalogue of those things for which he can praise them, Ellicott concludes, and then in the following verses shows how such conduct cannot be worthy of praise, being entirely at variance with the solemn and sacred circumstances in which the Lord's Supper originated. A.T. Robertson says the adjective rendered the Lord's is not just a biblical or ecclesiastical word, for it is found in the inscriptions and papyri in the sense of imperial, as in imperial finance and imperial treasury, and that it is possible the term applies both to the Love-feast, a sort of church supper held in connection with the Lord's Supper, and to the Eucharist; the word for supper, so common in the Gospels, occurs only here in Paul, and the selfish conduct of the Corinthians made it impossible to eat a Lord's Supper at all. The verb rendered taketh before means to take before others, Robertson says, and it was conduct like this that led to the complete separation between the Love-feast and the Lord's Supper: it was not even a common meal together, not to say a Lord's supper, but a mere grab-game, nothing being left for the hungry man at the love-feast, while such disgusting conduct as drunkenness was considered shameful even in heathen club suppers; Robertson quotes the summary of Robertson and Plummer, that here were hungry poor meeting intoxicated rich, at what was supposed to be a supper of the Lord. The double negative in the single question is an idiom, Robertson says, so that the sense is, for do you fail to have houses? Paul is not approving gluttony and drunkenness but only expressing horror at their sacrilege in despising the church of God; those that have not are not those without houses but those who have nothing, the have-nots in Findlay's phrase, in contrast with the men of property; and the closing question, what shall I say to you, is a deliberative subjunctive that well expresses Paul's bewilderment. Albert Barnes says that their coming together was not to eat the Lord's Supper, since the design of that ordinance was wholly lost in the manner of their observance; that the rich brought their own provisions and consumed them, so that the poor were left destitute; and that to shame them that have not is to put to the blush those who are poor, and who are unable to provide for themselves as the others had done.

debates: Where the love-feast came from and whether it is in view here: Calvin reports Chrysostom's derivation from the common meals of the first believers, cites Tertullian for its antiquity and Pliny's letter to Trajan for the Bithynian Christians' innocent repast in common, and adds his own conjecture that it arose from the sacrificial feasts of Jews and Gentiles, Christians correcting the faults while retaining a resemblance; Lightfoot disputes the identification altogether, wondering that the love-feasts of Jude should be expounded from this place, and citing Beza and Baronius as those who join them; Robertson takes the term as possibly covering both the love-feast and the Eucharist

What Paul means by saying it is not the Lord's Supper: Calvin denies that a single abuse annulled the institution and holds only that they polluted it, on the principle that a thing is not done at all if it is not done aright, while noting that others read it as meaning that it is not lawful for them to eat; Ellicott makes it a statement of impossibility, that with such divisions they cannot partake of the supper dedicated to the Lord; Gill says the ordinance was so abused that it lost the name; Robertson says their selfish conduct made it impossible to eat a Lord's Supper at all

Who the have-nots are: Clarke says they are not those who happened to be without victuals that day but those so poor as to be incapable of furnishing themselves as others had done; Robertson agrees, following Findlay, that they are not those without houses but those who have nothing, set against the men of property; Ellicott makes them the majority of the congregation, who came expecting to share in what the wealthier ought to have contributed

Calvin's characterisation of the argument from antiquity, that the thing is ancient and was done long ago and should therefore carry the weight of a revelation from heaven
Pliny's report to Trajan, quoted by Calvin, that the Christians of Bithynia affirmed under examination that they used to depart and come together again to take an innocent repast in common
Robertson's evidence from inscriptions and papyri that the adjective rendered the Lord's was in ordinary use for imperial, as of the imperial treasury
Robertson's summary of the scene as a mere grab-game, and the quoted description of hungry poor meeting intoxicated rich at what was supposed to be a supper of the Lord
Robertson's note that Paul's closing question is a deliberative subjunctive expressing bewilderment rather than instruction
Ellicott's observation that the poor man's shame is doubled, coming both from the contrast with wealth and from the evident dislike of the rich to eat with him
