23.pericope_label: Paul recites what he received of the Lord: that on the night of the betrayal Jesus took bread, gave thanks, brake it and said, This is my body, which is for you; this do in remembrance of me

schools.summary: John Gill says the apostle, having reproved the abuse, now sets before them the institution itself as he had received it from Christ, not by the report of others but by immediate revelation; that the night in which he was betrayed is mentioned to fix the time and to aggravate the ingratitude of those who abuse so solemn a memorial; and that the bread was taken, blessed and broken in the sight of the disciples, the breaking being significant of the sufferings of Christ. John Calvin says that hitherto the apostle has been exposing the abuse, and now proceeds to show the proper method of rectifying it, for the institution of Christ is a sure rule, so that if you turn aside from it but a very little you are out of the right course; hence, as the Corinthians had deviated from this rule, he calls them back to it. It is a passage that ought to be carefully observed, Calvin says, as showing that there is no remedy for correcting and purging out abuses short of a return to God's pure institution: thus the Lord himself, when discoursing respecting marriage, and the Scribes brought forward custom and also the permission given by Moses, simply brings forward his Father's institution as being an inviolable law. When we do this at the present day the Papists cry out that we are leaving nothing untouched, Calvin says; we openly demonstrate that it is not in one point merely that they have degenerated from our Lord's first institution but that they have corrupted it in a thousand ways, nothing being more manifest than that their Mass is diametrically opposed to the sacred Supper of our Lord. Calvin goes farther and says they show in the plainest manner that it is full of wicked abominations, so that there is need of reformation; and they demand, what it appears Paul had recourse to, that our Lord's institution be the common rule, to which both sides agree to make their appeal, which the Papists oppose with all their might. In these words the apostle intimates that there is no authority that is of any avail in the Church but that of the Lord alone, Calvin says: he has not delivered to them an invention of his own, nor contrived a new kind of supper according to his own humour, but has Christ as his authority in the way of handing it over, so that returning to the original source and bidding adieu to human laws, the authority of Christ will be maintained in its stability. The circumstance as to time instructs us as to the design of the sacrament, that the benefit of Christ's death may be ratified in us, Calvin says, for the Lord might have some time previously committed to the Apostles this covenant-seal, but he waited until the time of his oblation, that the Apostles might see soon after accomplished in reality in his body what he had represented to them in the bread and the cup. Should any one infer from this that the Supper ought therefore to be celebrated at night and after a bodily repast, Calvin answers that in what our Lord did we must consider what there is that he would have to be done by us: it is certain that he did not mean to institute a kind of nightly festival like that in honour of Ceres, and further that it was not his design to invite his people to come to this spiritual banquet with a well-filled stomach, so that such actions of Christ as are not intended for our imitation should not be reckoned as belonging to his institution. In this way there is no difficulty in setting aside that subtilty of Papists by which they shift off what has been stated as to the duty of maintaining Christ's institution in its simplicity, Calvin says, when they answer that they will therefore receive the Lord's Supper only at night, and take it not when fasting but after having dined: all this is mere trifling, for it is easy to distinguish what our Lord did in order that we might imitate it. On the giving of thanks Calvin says that every gift we receive from the hand of God is sanctified to us by the word and prayer, and that we nowhere read that the Lord tasted bread along with his disciples without mention being made of his giving thanks, by which example he has assuredly instructed us to do the like; this thanksgiving, however, has a reference to something higher, for Christ gave thanks to the Father for his mercy towards the human race and the inestimable benefit of redemption, and he invites us by his example to raise up our minds as often as we approach the sacred table to an acknowledgment of the boundless love of God towards us. We must take notice that Christ here distributes the bread among the Apostles, that all may partake of it in common, and thus every one may have his portion, that there may be an equal participation among all, Calvin says; accordingly, when there is not a table in common prepared for all the pious, and where believers do not mutually participate, it is to no purpose that the name of the Lord's Supper is laid claim to. But for what purpose are the people called to mass, Calvin asks, unless it be that they may go away empty from an unmeaning show, as if returning from a useless and foolish mountebank scene? It has therefore nothing in unison with the supper, and hence we infer that Christ's promise is no more applicable to the mass than to the feast of the Salii; for when Christ promises that he will give us his body, he at the same time commands us to take, and unless we obey this command it is to no purpose that we glory in his promise, the promise being annexed to the commandment in a conditional way.

Matthew Henry says the apostle here sets before the Corinthians the divine institution of the ordinance, the best remedy against their abuse of it, and one which he had received from the Lord himself: the time is marked, the same night in which he was betrayed, which should raise the most tender thoughts in every communicant, since our Lord was then in the depth of his sorrows and yet mindful of his church to the end. Henry observes that the breaking of the bread was significant of the breaking of Christ's body for us, that the giving of thanks teaches us with what temper we should approach the table, and that the command to do this in remembrance of him makes the ordinance a memorial, appointed to keep the death of Christ in continual view until his coming again. John Lightfoot, annotating in his usual manner from the Jewish sources, observes that when our Lord delivered to them that institution they might observe that the scope and end of it was the commemoration of him, and sets the Christian rite beside the paschal usages with which the disciples were familiar.

Adam Clarke says the papists believe the apostles were not ordained priests before these words, and quotes the canon of the Council of Trent, that if any one shall say that in these words, this do in remembrance of me, Christ did not ordain his apostles priests, let him be accursed; and Clarke answers that he who does believe such an absurdity, on such a ground, is contemptible. Clarke observes further that the apostle grounds the whole of the correction on the original institution, which he had received from the Lord, and that the words of institution are recited exactly in order that the Corinthians might see how far their practice had departed from what was delivered to them. John Wesley says that Paul received of the Lord, by an immediate revelation, what he also delivered to them, so that the account rests on the highest authority; that the Lord Jesus, the same night in which he was betrayed, when his enemies were preparing and his own disciple was selling him, took bread, and having given thanks brake it, the breaking being an emblem of his sufferings; and that this do in remembrance of me appoints the ordinance as a standing memorial, the whole design of it being to keep in mind the love of Christ in dying for us until he come.

Charles Ellicott asks whether the words imply that St. Paul had a direct revelation from Christ of the words and facts which he now recalls, or merely that he knew from the accounts given him by others what took place on that solemn occasion; the whole structure of the passage seems to imply that what follows had been received directly from Christ, and that he is not appealing to a well-known tradition, in which case he would scarcely have used the singular I received, nor to something learnt from the other Apostles, in which case he would not have said I emphatically, nor from the Lord, for the other Apostles had not received their knowledge of these facts from the Lord but from their own observation and hearing. How Christ thus communicated these truths to his new Apostle we are not told, Ellicott says, and the method of communication does not appear to cause either doubt or difficulty to those to whom the Apostle conveyed the information. The Apostle was not now for the first time communicating these facts to the Corinthians, Ellicott says: he had told them all this before, and therefore they were sinning against knowledge when they degraded a feast which they knew to be so solemn. Comparing the account with the Gospel narratives, Ellicott notes that Matthew and Mark wrote many years after and recorded what they remembered, while St. Paul writes within a very few years of having received it an account of what had been directly communicated by the Lord, and that this was most probably the first written record of what occurred on that night. The fact that St. Luke's narrative agrees most closely with St. Paul's would imply, not as some rationalising critics insinuate that St. Paul was indebted to St. Luke, but that St. Luke attached high value to an account which his companion had received directly from the glorified Christ, Ellicott says; the suggestion that St. Luke copied his account of the Last Supper from this Epistle is a mere speculation and in the highest degree improbable, for if that Evangelist had used this Epistle in writing his Gospel, is it likely that he would have been content with giving the somewhat scanty account of our Lord's appearances after his resurrection when he had at hand the much ampler record of the appearance to the five hundred brethren and to James which this Epistle contains? In all the narratives the outlines of the scene are the same, Ellicott says, and there can be no mistake as to their all being truthful and, as the minor discrepancies prove, honestly independent records of an actual historical scene. It is worthy of remark that in the heated controversies which have raged around the Eucharistic Feast as to its spiritual significance, its evidential value has been frequently lost sight of, Ellicott says: if the Betrayal and Crucifixion are not historical facts, how can we account for the existence of the Eucharistic Feast? Here is an Epistle whose authenticity the most searching and ruthless criticism has never disputed, and we have evidence of the existence of this feast and its connection with events which occurred only twenty years before. If we bear in mind that the Apostles were Jews, and yet spoke of that wine which they drank as blood, and that they were lovingly devoted to the person of Christ and yet spake of that bread which they ate as his flesh, can the wildest imagination conceive of that practice having originated with themselves as their most solemn religious rite, Ellicott asks, and could anything but the record given in the Gospel narrative possibly account for such a ceremony holding such a place in a sect composed of Christianised Jews? A dark conspiracy like that of Catiline might have selected the tasting of human blood as the symbol of the conspirators' sanguinary hate of all human order and life, Ellicott says, but such a band of men as the early Christians certainly could not of their own thought have made such a choice and publicly proclaimed it; and if this be true, if Jesus, the night before an ignominious death, instituted this strange and solemn rite which has been handed down century after century in unbroken continuity, can that foresight as to the future of his Church be assigned to one who was less than what Christendom claims her Lord to be? When Christ died his Apostles gave up all as lost and went back sorrowfully to their old work as fishermen, Ellicott concludes: Christendom was not an afterthought of the Apostles, but the forethought of the Lord. The words the same night in which he was betrayed imply that the history of the Betrayal was familiar, Ellicott adds, and they also solemnly and touchingly remind the Corinthians of the strange contrast between the events of that night and the scenes in which they indulge now. On the next verse Ellicott renders it better, and having given thanks, he brake it and said, this is my body which is for you, and says the insertion of the words take, eat, and of the word broken, is not supported by manuscript evidence: the former were probably inserted so as to produce a verbal identity with St. Matthew's account, and the word broken possibly as explanatory, since at the institution the act of breaking the bread explained sufficiently what was meant. This do in remembrance of me means all that was done then, Ellicott says: bless the bread, break it, distribute it, eat it, for when I am no longer with you bodily these acts will make memory grow into realisation of my presence in your midst; if the soft music of those words could reach us now, disentangled from the theological discords of intervening ages, surely they would come to us with some such significance, and to those who first heard them they certainly must have implied not that a physical presence was about to be perpetuated, but rather that there was now something for them which would in after ages console them for a physical absence. A.T. Robertson says the words are a direct claim to revelation from the Lord Jesus on the origin of the Lord's Supper, that Luke's account is almost identical with this one and that he could easily have read this epistle before he wrote his Gospel; Paul received the account from the Lord and passed it on from himself to them, a true tradition in the sense already used in this chapter. The participle rendered when he had given thanks is from the verb from which our word Eucharist comes, Robertson says; and the word broken of the received text is clearly not genuine, Luke having given, which is the real idea here, for as a matter of fact the body of Jesus was not broken, the bread being broken but not the body. The phrase in remembrance of me shows the objective use of the possessive pronoun, Robertson says: not my remembrance of you, but your remembrance of me, the noun being an old word occurring in the New Testament only here and in Luke. Albert Barnes says the apostle appeals to the original institution as the standard by which their conduct is to be judged, and that the design of the ordinance is commemorative, appointed to keep in perpetual remembrance the fact that the body of Christ was given for us.

Cyril of Jerusalem says that even of itself the teaching of the Blessed Paul is sufficient to give full assurance concerning those Divine Mysteries, of which, having been deemed worthy, the hearers are become of the same body and blood with Christ. For you have just heard him say distinctly, Cyril says, that our Lord Jesus Christ in the night in which he was betrayed took bread, and when he had given thanks he brake it and gave to his disciples, saying, Take, eat, this is my Body; and having taken the cup and given thanks, he said, Take, drink, this is my Blood. Since then he himself declared and said of the Bread, this is my Body, who shall dare to doubt any longer, Cyril asks; and since he has himself affirmed and said, this is my Blood, who shall ever hesitate, saying that it is not his blood?

debates: Whether Paul had the account by revelation or by report: Ellicott argues from the emphatic I, the singular verb and the phrase from the Lord that it must be direct revelation, since the other apostles knew these things by observation and not from the Lord; Robertson calls it a direct claim to revelation in a single line; Calvin uses the clause for a different purpose, to establish that no authority avails in the Church but the Lord's, since Paul contrived nothing of his own

How Paul's account stands to Luke's: Ellicott holds that Luke valued an account received directly from the glorified Christ, denies that Paul was indebted to Luke as rationalising critics insinuate, and argues that had Luke used this epistle he would not have left so scanty a record of the resurrection appearances with the fuller account of the five hundred and of James at hand; Robertson says without heat that Luke could easily have read this epistle before writing his Gospel

What the words this is my body imply about presence: Ellicott says that to those who first heard them they must have implied not a physical presence perpetuated but something to console them for a physical absence, and wishes the words could be heard free of the theological discords of later ages; Cyril takes them the opposite way, arguing that since Christ himself declared it, none may dare to doubt or hesitate to call the cup his blood; Calvin, without settling the question here, insists that the promise is annexed to the command, so that without the taking there is nothing to glory in

Whether the circumstances of the night bind us: Calvin answers the inference that the Supper must be kept at night after a meal by distinguishing what our Lord did from what he meant us to do, since he did not institute a nightly festival like that of Ceres nor invite men to a spiritual banquet with a full stomach; Clarke turns the same principle against the canon of Trent which makes the words of institution an ordination of priests
outliers: Ellicott's evidential argument, that if the Betrayal and Crucifixion are not historical the existence of the Eucharistic feast cannot be accounted for, and that Jews devoted to Christ could not of their own thought have made the drinking of blood their most solemn rite
Ellicott's comparison with the conspiracy of Catiline, which might have chosen the tasting of human blood as a symbol where the early Christians could not
Ellicott's conclusion that Christendom was not an afterthought of the Apostles but the forethought of the Lord
Ellicott's wish that the soft music of the words of institution could reach us disentangled from the theological discords of intervening ages
Robertson's point that the bread was broken but the body of Jesus was not, so that the received reading broken cannot stand
Robertson's note that the remembrance intended is the objective one, our remembrance of him and not his of us
Calvin's comparison of the mass to the sumptuous feast of the Salii, the priests of Mars, as equally remote from Christ's promise
Clarke's retort to the Tridentine canon, that whoever believes such an absurdity on such a ground is contemptible

25.pericope_label: The cup taken after supper, the new covenant in Christ’s blood, and the declaration that as often as they eat this bread and drink this cup they show the Lord’s death till he come

schools.summary: John Gill says the cup was taken after supper, that is, after the paschal supper was ended, which shows that the Lord's supper is a distinct ordinance and not to be confounded with a common meal; that the cup is called the new testament or covenant in Christ's blood because it is the sign and seal of that covenant which is ratified by his blood; and that the words as often as ye drink it suppose a frequent repetition of the ordinance, though no set time is fixed. Gill takes showing the Lord's death to mean a declaring and publishing of it, both to God and before men, and till he come to mean until his second coming, so that the ordinance is to continue in the church to the end of the world. John Calvin says the Apostle seems to intimate that there was some interval of time between the distribution of the bread and that of the cup, and it does not quite appear from the Evangelists whether the whole of the transaction was continuous; this, however, is of no great moment, for it may be that the Lord delivered in the meantime some address, after distributing the bread and before giving the cup, and as he did or said nothing that was not in harmony with the sacrament, we need not say that the administration of it was disturbed or interrupted. What is affirmed as to the bread is applicable also to the cup, Calvin says, and thus by this form of expression he intimates what he had before stated more briefly, that the cup is the covenant, which has been once confirmed by the offering up of his body and is now confirmed by eating, when believers feast upon that sacrifice; accordingly, while Paul and Luke use the one expression, Matthew and Mark employ another, which amounts to the same thing, for the blood was poured out to reconcile us to God, and now we drink of it in a spiritual sense that we may be partakers of reconciliation. Hence in the Supper we have both a covenant and a confirmatory pledge of the covenant, Calvin says. It is well known that sacraments receive that name from being seals of the divine will, to confirm it in our minds, Calvin continues: for as a covenant is entered into among men with solemn rites, so it is in the same manner that the Lord deals with us, and in consequence of the connection between the word and the sign, the covenant of the Lord is really included in the sacraments. This will be of no small importance for understanding the nature of the sacraments, Calvin says, for if they are covenants then they contain promises by which consciences may be roused up to an assurance of salvation, whence it follows that they are not merely outward signs of profession before men but are inwardly too helps to faith. Christ then has appointed a two-fold sign in the Supper, Calvin says: what God hath joined together let not man put asunder, and to distribute the bread without the cup is to mutilate Christ's institution; for we hear Christ's words, and as he commands us to eat of the bread so he commands us to drink of the cup, and to obey the one half of the command and neglect the other half, what is this but to make sport of his commandment? To keep back the people from that cup which Christ sets before all, after first drinking of it, as is done under the tyranny of the Pope, who can deny that this is diabolical presumption, Calvin asks; and as to the cavil that Christ spoke merely to the Apostles and not to the common people, it is exceedingly childish and is easily refuted from this passage, for Paul here addresses himself to men and women indiscriminately and to the whole body of the Church, and declares that he had delivered this to them agreeably to the commandment of the Lord. By what spirit will those pretend to be actuated who have dared to set aside this ordinance, Calvin asks; yet even at this day this gross abuse is obstinately defended, and what occasion is there for wonder if they endeavour impudently to excuse by words and writings what they so cruelly maintain by fire and sword? Paul now adds what kind of remembrance ought to be cherished, that is, with thanksgiving, Calvin says; not that the remembrance consists wholly in confession with the mouth, for the chief thing is that the efficacy of Christ's death be sealed in our consciences, but this knowledge should stir us up to a confession in respect of praise, so as to declare before men what we feel inwardly before God. The Supper then is a kind of memorial which must always remain in the Church until the last coming of Christ, Calvin concludes, and it has been appointed for this purpose, that Christ may put us in mind of the benefit of his death and that we may recognise it before men, whence it has the name of the Eucharist.

John Lightfoot says it is known what the declaration in the Passover supper was, namely a declaration of the great works of God in the deliverance of the people out of Egypt. The same, as it seems, would these Judaizing Corinthians retain in the Lord's supper, Lightfoot says, as if the Eucharist were instituted and superadded only for that commemoration; and the Greek word rendered ye do show answers very well to the Hebrew word for the declaration, so that while the apostle admonishes them that the death of Christ is that which is to be declared, it may be gathered that they erred in this very thing and looked some other way. Lightfoot's annotation on the covenant in the preceding verse turns on the rabbinic usage of the word for a covenant or bequest, and sets the Jewish forms of solemn giving beside the apostle's language.

Adam Clarke says that as in the passover they showed forth the bondage they had been in and the redemption they had received from it, so in the eucharist they showed forth the sacrificial death of Christ and the redemption from sin derived from it. John Wesley says that the cup was taken after supper, and that therefore we ought not to confound this with a common meal; and that on the words do this in remembrance of me it is to be observed that the ancient sacrifices were in remembrance of sin, whereas this sacrifice, once offered, is still represented in remembrance of the remission of sins. Ye show forth the Lord's death means ye proclaim, as it were, and openly avow it to God and to all the world, Wesley says, and till he come means till he come in glory.

Charles Ellicott says we have here an intimation not found in St. Matthew or St. Mark's narrative, that the blessing of the cup took place after supper, which implies that the blessing of the bread took place earlier in the meal. This cup is the new testament is better rendered, this cup is the new covenant, Ellicott says: the word new is peculiar to this and St. Luke's narrative and does not occur in the best manuscripts of St. Matthew and St. Mark; the new covenant of grace between God and humanity was ratified in the blood of Christ, and the cup containing the symbol of that blood is therefore the pledge and witness of that covenant, a new covenant in blood as contrasted with the old covenant in blood at Sinai. The words as oft as ye drink can scarcely be taken as a command to make all occasions of bodily refreshment virtually a eucharist, Ellicott says, but must be regarded as referring definitely to this particular rite. The previous verse concluded the account of the institution as conveyed by Christ to St. Paul, and the Apostle himself now again speaks, Ellicott says: all this being the true account of the origin of this Supper, as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, as distinct from other bread and wine, you proclaim the Lord's death until he come. The Greek word for ye show is that used for making a public oral proclamation, Ellicott says, and the passage does not imply, as some have suggested, that the Lord's Supper was a living sermon or an acted discourse, but, as is still the custom, that when the bread and wine were consecrated to this sacred use there was an oral declaration made, perhaps in the very words the Apostle here uses, of the facts of the original institution; the imperative form given in the margin of the Authorised version is quite inadmissible. In the pathetic words until he come we may find an expression of the belief, perhaps largely due to the hope, that the Second Advent was not far distant, Ellicott concludes. A.T. Robertson says the phrase after supper is the preposition with the articular aorist infinitive, after the dining, as in Luke; that the position of the verb before the words in my blood makes it a secondary or additional predicate, not to be taken merely with the word covenant; and that as oft as ye drink it is the usual construction for a general temporal clause of repetition. Till he come is a common idiom with the aorist subjunctive for future time, Robertson says, Luke using a different particle; and the Lord's Supper is the great preacher of the death of Christ till his second coming. Albert Barnes says the cup is called the new covenant because it is the seal or ratification of it, and that the ordinance is designed to be a standing memorial in the church, its perpetuity being fixed by the words till he come, which imply both that the Lord is now absent and that he will certainly return.

debates: What showing the Lord's death means: Ellicott says the Greek word is that for a public oral proclamation and expressly denies that the Supper is a living sermon or an acted discourse, holding that an oral declaration of the institution accompanied the consecration; Robertson takes the rejected view outright, calling the Supper the great preacher of the death of Christ till his second coming; Clarke and Wesley take it as an open avowal before God and the world

Why the point about what is declared needed making: Lightfoot argues that the Passover supper had its own set declaration of the deliverance from Egypt, and that the Judaizing Corinthians appear to have retained that declaration in the Lord's supper as though the Eucharist were added only for it, so that the apostle's insistence on the death of Christ shows where they erred; Clarke draws the parallel between passover and eucharist without making it an error; Calvin makes the remembrance one of thanksgiving, whence the name Eucharist

Whether both kinds belong to all: Calvin argues from the two-fold sign that to give the bread without the cup mutilates the institution, since obeying half a command is to make sport of it, and answers the plea that Christ spoke only to the Apostles by pointing out that Paul here addresses men and women indiscriminately and the whole body of the Church; the other voices treat the two elements together without raising the question

How far as oft as ye drink extends: Ellicott denies it can make every occasion of bodily refreshment a eucharist and restricts it to this rite; Robertson treats it simply as a general temporal clause of repetition; Gill takes it to imply frequent repetition without fixing any set time
outliers: Calvin's principle that sacraments are covenants and therefore contain promises, so that they are not merely outward signs of profession before men but inwardly helps to faith
Calvin's closing question, what wonder it is that men should impudently excuse in words and writings what they cruelly maintain by fire and sword
Lightfoot's identification of the Greek word for showing with the Hebrew term for the Passover declaration
Ellicott's note that new is peculiar to this account and Luke's and is absent from the best manuscripts of Matthew and Mark
Ellicott's suggestion that until he come expresses a belief, perhaps largely due to the hope, that the Second Advent was not far distant
Wesley's contrast that the ancient sacrifices were in remembrance of sin while this one is in remembrance of the remission of sins

27.pericope_label: Whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup unworthily is guilty of the body and blood of the Lord; let a man examine himself, for he that eats and drinks without discerning the body eats and drinks judgment to himself

schools.summary: John Gill says that to eat and drink unworthily is not to be understood of a want of personal worthiness, for then none could partake at all, but of an unworthy manner of eating and drinking, such as that of the Corinthians, who came without reverence and without regard to the design of the ordinance; and that to be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord is to be chargeable with a profanation of that which represents them. Gill takes the examination required to be of a man's state and of his faith, and the eating and drinking of judgment to be temporal chastisement rather than final condemnation, as the following verses show. Not discerning the Lord's body means not distinguishing between the bread of the ordinance and common bread, Gill says, nor considering what it signifies, namely the body of Christ given for his people. John Calvin says that if the Lord requires gratitude from us in the receiving of this sacrament, and would have us acknowledge his grace with the heart and publish it with the mouth, that man will not go unpunished who has put insult upon him rather than honour, for the Lord will not allow his commandment to be despised. Some restrict the unworthiness to the Corinthians and the abuse that had crept in among them, Calvin says, but he is of opinion that Paul here, according to his usual manner, passed on from the particular case to a general statement, or from one instance to an entire class: there was one fault that prevailed among the Corinthians, and he takes occasion from this to speak of every kind of faulty administration or reception of the Supper. To eat unworthily, then, is to pervert the pure and right use of it by our abuse of it, Calvin says, and hence there are various degrees of this unworthiness, some offending more grievously and others less so: one intrudes himself without repentance while addicted to open vice, and as such downright contempt is a token of wanton insult against Christ, there can be no doubt that such a person receives the Supper to his own destruction; another comes forward who is not addicted to any open or flagrant vice but is not so prepared in heart as became him, and as this carelessness is a sign of irreverence it is also deserving of punishment from God. Now this passage gave rise to a question which some afterwards agitated with too much keenness, whether the wicked really partake of the Lord's body, Calvin says: some were led by the heat of controversy so far as to say that it was received indiscriminately by the good and the bad, and many at this day maintain pertinaciously and most clamorously that in the first Supper Peter received no more than Judas. It is indeed with reluctance that Calvin disputes keenly with any one on this point, which is in his opinion not an essential one, but as others allow themselves without reason to pronounce with a magisterial air whatever may seem good to them, and to launch out thunderbolts upon every one that mutters anything to the contrary, he will be excused if he calmly adduces reasons in support of what he reckons to be true. Calvin holds it as a settled point, and will not allow himself to be driven from it, that Christ cannot be disjoined from his Spirit; hence he maintains that his body is not received as dead, or even inactive, disjoined from the grace and power of his Spirit. In what way could the man who is altogether destitute of a living faith and repentance, having nothing of the Spirit of Christ, receive Christ himself, Calvin asks; nay more, as he is entirely under the influence of Satan and sin, how will he be capable of receiving Christ? While therefore Calvin acknowledges that there are some who receive Christ truly in the Supper and yet at the same time unworthily, as is the case with many weak persons, he does not admit that those who bring with them a mere historical faith, without a lively feeling of repentance and faith, receive anything but the sign; for he cannot endure to maim Christ.

John Lightfoot says that not discerning the body is to be meant of the proper act of the understanding, that is, of the true judgment concerning the nature and signification of the sacrament. If it were said, not discerning the Lord, it might be rendered in the same sense as he knew not the Lord, that is, he loves him not, he fears him not, he worships him not, Lightfoot says; but when it is said, not discerning the body, it plainly speaks of the act of the understanding, that he does not rightly distinguish of the body of the Lord. And this was a grievous error of these Judaizing Corinthians, Lightfoot says, who would see nothing of the body of Christ in the Eucharist, or of his death, their eyes being too intent upon the commemoration of the Passover: they retained the old leaven of Judaism in this new Passover of the Eucharist, and this was their partaking of the sacrament unworthily, as assigning it a scope and end much too unworthy and much too mean. On the earlier verses Lightfoot notes that the apostle explains himself as he goes, and that his warning about unworthiness is to be read by the light of what he says here about the understanding.

Adam Clarke says that to put a final end to controversies relative to these words, the reader should observe that to eat and drink the bread and wine in the Lord's Supper unworthily is to eat and drink as the Corinthians did, who ate it not in reference to Jesus Christ's sacrificial death, but rather in such a way as the Israelites did the passover, which they celebrated in remembrance of their deliverance from Egyptian bondage. Likewise these mongrel Christians at Corinth used it as a kind of historical commemoration of the death of Christ, Clarke says, and did not in the whole institution discern the Lord's body and blood as a sacrificial offering for sin; and besides, in their celebration of it they acted in a way utterly unbecoming the gravity of a sacred ordinance. Those who acknowledge it as a sacrificial offering, and receive it in remembrance of God's love in sending his Son into the world, can neither bring damnation upon themselves by so doing nor eat nor drink unworthily, Clarke says. To be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord means that if a man use it irreverently, and deny that Christ suffered unjustly, he in effect joins issue with the Jews in their condemnation and crucifixion of the Lord Jesus, and renders himself guilty of the death of our blessed Lord, Clarke says; though some understand the passage to mean that he eats and drinks unworthily and brings on himself the punishment mentioned in the next verse. Let a man examine himself, that is, let him try whether he has proper faith in the Lord Jesus, and whether he discerns the Lord's body, and whether he duly considers that the bread and wine point out the crucified body and spilt blood of Christ, Clarke says. Eateth and drinketh damnation means judgment or punishment, Clarke insists, and yet this is not unto damnation, for the judgment or punishment inflicted upon the disorderly and the profane was intended for their emendation, since it is afterwards said that when we are judged we are chastened, corrected as a father does his children, that we should not be condemned with the world. John Wesley says that whosoever eats and drinks unworthily, that is, in an unworthy, irreverent manner, without regard to him whose institution it is or to the end for which it was appointed, is guilty of profaning that which represents the body and blood of the Lord; that a man should examine himself as to his knowledge, his faith and his repentance, and so eat; and that he who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment to himself, not discerning the Lord's body, that is, not putting a difference between this and common food.

Charles Ellicott says the verse is better rendered, whosoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord, since the entire weight of manuscript evidence is in favour of the conjunction or and not and, which was probably retained in the English version lest the disjunctive might seem to favour the practice of receiving in one kind only. It is clear, however, that if in these early days there was a considerable interval between the receiving of the bread and the wine, it would have been quite possible for a partaker to have received one only unworthily, and the Apostle intimates that in either case he is guilty, Ellicott says: sin was the cause of that body being broken and that blood shed, and therefore the one who unworthily uses the symbols of them becomes a participator in the very guilt of those who crucified that body and shed that blood. So let him eat implies that a man should partake of this sacred feast only after he has carefully examined himself as to the spirit in which he approaches such holy bread and wine, Ellicott says. The word unworthily is not in the best Greek manuscripts of the twenty-ninth verse, Ellicott notes, and the Greek word rendered damnation does not imply final condemnation: on the contrary it only means such temporal judgments as the sickness and weakness subsequently mentioned, which are to save the man from sharing the final damnation of the heathen. The words the Lord's are also to be omitted, the weight of manuscript evidence being altogether against their authenticity, Ellicott says, and the following verse is a parenthesis, so that the force of the passage is that he who eats and drinks without discerning the Body, that is, the Church, in that assembly, eats and drinks a judgment to himself. There are some important points to be borne in mind regarding this interpretation, Ellicott says. First, the Greek word which we render discerning signifies to arrive at a right estimate of the character or quality of a thing. Secondly, the fault which St. Paul was condemning was the practice which the Corinthians had fallen into of regarding these gatherings as opportunities for individual indulgence and not as Church assemblies: they did not rightly estimate such gatherings as being corporate meetings, nor themselves as being no longer isolated individuals but members of the common Body, and they ought to discern in these meetings of the Church a body and in themselves parts of a body. Not only is this the most accurate and literal interpretation of the Greek, Ellicott ventures to think, but it is the only view which seems to make the passage bear intelligibly on the point which St. Paul is considering and the real evil which he seeks to counteract. Thirdly, to refer these words directly or indirectly to the question of a physical presence in the Lord's Supper is to divorce them violently from their surroundings, and to make them allude to some evil for which the explicit and practical remedy commended at the end of the chapter would be no remedy at all, Ellicott says; moreover, if the word body means the Lord's physical body, surely the word Lord's would have been added, and the words and the blood, for the non-recognition of the blood would be just as great an offence. Fourthly, St. Paul never uses the word body in reference to our Lord's physical body without some clear indication that such is meant, Ellicott says, whereas the use of the word Body, or Body of Christ, meaning the Church, is frequent, and we have had it but a few verses before in reference to this very subject. A.T. Robertson says the adverb rendered unworthily is an old adverb occurring only here in the New Testament and is not genuine in the twenty-ninth verse, Paul defining his own meaning as he goes; he does not say or imply that we ourselves must be worthy to partake of the Lord's Supper, for no one would ever partake on those terms, and many pious souls have abstained from observing the ordinance through false exegesis here. Shall be guilty means shall be held guilty of a crime committed against the body and blood of the Lord by such sacrilege, Robertson says. Let a man prove himself means test himself as he would a piece of metal to see if it is genuine, and such examination of one's motives would have made impossible the disgraceful scenes described earlier, Robertson says. If he discern not the body is a conditional use of the participle, not judging the body, so that he eats and drinks judgment on himself, Robertson says: the verb is an old and common word, our discriminate, to distinguish, and eating the bread and drinking the wine as symbols of the Lord's body and blood in death probes one's heart to the very depths. Albert Barnes says that to partake unworthily is to partake in a manner unsuitable to the design of the ordinance, and that the guilt spoken of is the guilt of profaning what represents the body and blood of the Lord; that the self-examination enjoined is a solemn duty binding on all who approach the table; and that the judgment threatened is not eternal condemnation but the temporal chastisement which the following verses describe.

John Chrysostom asks what these words mean, when another object is proposed to us, and answers that this is Paul's custom, not only to treat of those things which he had proposed to himself, but also, if an argument incidental to his purpose occur, to proceed upon this also with great diligence, and especially when it relates to very necessary and urgent matters. Thus, when he was discoursing with married persons and the question about the servants fell in his way, he handled it very strenuously and at great length, Chrysostom says; and again, when he was speaking of the duty of not going to law before those courts, then also, having fallen upon the admonition respecting covetousness, he discoursed at length concerning this subject likewise. Now the same thing he has also done here, Chrysostom says: having once found occasion to remind them of the Mysteries, he judged it necessary to proceed with that subject, for indeed it was no ordinary one, wherefore also he discoursed very awfully concerning it, providing for that which is the sum of all good things, namely their approaching those Mysteries with a pure conscience.

debates: What body is meant in the last verse: Ellicott, dropping the words the Lord's as unsupported, argues in four steps that it is the Church, since the verb means to arrive at a right estimate, since the fault was treating corporate assemblies as occasions of private indulgence, since referring the words to a physical presence would leave the practical remedy at the end of the chapter no remedy at all and would require the blood to be named as well, and since Paul never uses body of Christ's physical body without clear indication; Lightfoot makes it an act of the understanding, a right judgment of the nature and signification of the sacrament; Clarke and Lightfoot agree that the offenders were Judaizers who saw only a commemoration like the Passover and not a sacrificial offering; Gill, Barnes and Wesley take it as putting a difference between this bread and common food

What the judgment threatened is: Ellicott says the Greek does not imply final condemnation but the temporal judgments named in the next verse, meant to save the man from the final damnation of the heathen; Clarke presses the same, that the punishment was for the emendation of the disorderly, who are chastened as a father corrects his children; Barnes and Gill agree, so that the rendering damnation is unanimously set aside

Whether the wicked receive Christ's body: Calvin reports that some say it is received indiscriminately by good and bad, and that many maintain Peter received no more than Judas at the first Supper, and answers that Christ cannot be disjoined from his Spirit, so that a man wholly under the influence of Satan cannot receive him, and one who brings a merely historical faith receives nothing but the sign; he grants that weak believers may receive Christ truly and yet unworthily

How wide the warning reaches: Calvin holds that Paul passes from the particular Corinthian abuse to every kind of faulty administration or reception, with degrees of unworthiness according to the offence; Robertson insists the word does not require the communicant to be worthy, since on those terms none would ever partake, and blames a false exegesis here for keeping pious souls from the ordinance
outliers: Ellicott's suspicion that the English version kept the conjunction and rather than or lest the disjunctive should seem to favour communion in one kind
Robertson's pastoral observation that many pious souls have abstained from the ordinance through false exegesis of the word unworthily
Calvin's reluctance to dispute a point he does not think essential, and his complaint that others launch thunderbolts at any one who mutters a word against them
Calvin's refusal, in his own phrase, to maim Christ by allowing that his body could be received disjoined from his Spirit
Robertson's image of self-examination as testing a piece of metal to see whether it is genuine
Lightfoot's charge that the Corinthians retained the old leaven of Judaism in this new Passover of the Eucharist
Chrysostom's observation that Paul habitually pursues an incidental argument at length when it touches urgent matters

30.pericope_label: The weakness, sickness and death among them are chastisement, not final condemnation; if they judged themselves they would not be judged; therefore let them tarry one for another, and if any hunger let him eat at home

schools.summary: John Gill says that for this cause many are weak and sickly among you, and many sleep, is to be understood of bodily infirmities and death inflicted by God as a chastisement for their profanation of the ordinance; that if we would judge ourselves, that is, examine and condemn ourselves for our sins, we should not be judged, that is, not be thus corrected; and that when we are judged we are chastened of the Lord as a father chastens his children, that we should not be condemned with the world of the ungodly. Gill takes the direction to tarry one for another as requiring that all should partake together and in order, and the direction that a hungry man eat at home as separating the ordinance from any common meal. John Calvin says that from the discussion of a general doctrine the apostle returns to the particular subject with which he had set out, and comes to this conclusion, that equality must be observed in the Lord's Supper, that there may be a real participation as there ought to be, and that they may not celebrate every one his own supper; and further, that this sacrament ought not to be mixed up with common feasts. It is probable that there were some things in addition which it would be of advantage to put into better order, Calvin says, but as they were of less importance the Apostle delays the correction of them until his coming among them; it may be at the same time that there was nothing of this nature, but as one knows better what is necessary when he is present to see, Paul reserves to himself the liberty of arranging matters when present, according as occasion may require. Papists arm themselves against us with this buckler too, for defending their mass, Calvin says, for they interpret the rest to be the mass which Paul here promises, as if he would have taken the liberty of overturning that eternal appointment of Christ which he here so distinctly approves of; for what resemblance does the mass bear to Christ's institution? But away with such trifles, Calvin concludes, as it is certain that Paul speaks only of outward decorum, and as this is put in the power of the Church, so it ought to be arranged according to the condition of times, places and persons.

John Lightfoot says that the direction to tarry one for another is not that the apostle allowed those ante-suppers of the Judaizers, and commands the Gentile party of the church to wait till the Jewish part ate those suppers; but that, having before wholly condemned those paschal ante-suppers, he would take away all dividing into parties, and would have all resort to the Eucharist together with one accord, not separately, and in parts and contentions. Lightfoot's reading here completes the account he has given through the chapter, in which the Corinthian fault is traced to a Judaizing retention of paschal forms, and the apostle's remedy is the removal of everything that split the assembly into a Jewish and a Gentile part.

Adam Clarke says that for this cause, that is, because they partook of this sacred ordinance without discerning the Lord's body, many are weak and sickly; and it is hard to say whether these words refer to the consequences of their own intemperance or to some extraordinary disorders inflicted immediately by God himself. That there were disorders of the most reprehensible kind among these people at this sacred supper the preceding verses sufficiently point out, Clarke says, and after such excesses many might be weak and sickly among them, and many might sleep, that is, die, for continual experience shows us that many fall victims to their own intemperance; however, acting as they did in this solemn and awful sacrament, they might have provoked God to plague them with divers diseases and sundry kinds of death, as the Communion service has it. If we would judge ourselves means that if, having acted improperly, we condemn our conduct and humble ourselves, we shall not be judged, that is, punished for the sin we have committed, Clarke says. When ye come together to eat the Lord's Supper, tarry one for another, that is, do not eat and drink in parties as ye have done heretofore, and do not connect it with any other meal, Clarke says. John Wesley says that many are weak and sickly, and many sleep, means that these bodily disorders and deaths were the immediate consequence of their profanation of the ordinance; that if we would judge ourselves thoroughly we should not be thus judged; and that when we are judged we are chastened of the Lord, in mercy and not in wrath, that we should not be condemned with the world. Wesley takes the closing directions to mean that the Corinthians should wait for one another so that all might partake together, and that whoever is hungry should eat at home, so that they come together not to satisfy nature but for the ordinance itself.

Charles Ellicott says that for this cause, that is, because they do not regard these feasts to which the Lord's Supper is joined as gatherings in a common body, but eat and drink to excess and so gain no spiritual advantage but actually physical evil, many are weak and sickly; and that many sleep is better rendered, and some die, since even death sometimes resulted from their drunken orgies, either naturally or by God's direct visitation. The change to the first person, courteously identifying himself with them, is characteristic of St. Paul, Ellicott notes; and the following verse explicitly declares that the condemnation following an unworthy partaking was not final condemnation but temporal suffering, to save them from being condemned with the heathen. The rest, or literally the remaining matters, doubtless refers to some other details connected with the charity-feasts, Ellicott says. From the foregoing we gather the following outline of the method of celebration of the Lord's Supper in the Apostolic Church, Ellicott continues: it was a common practice amongst the Greeks at this time to hold a feast to which all contributed and of which all partook, and a similar arrangement soon sprang up in the Christian communities and was called the charity-feast. At these gatherings was celebrated, probably at first daily and afterwards weekly, the Lord's Supper, Ellicott says, and it consisted of two parts, a loaf broken and distributed during the meal, and a cup partaken of by all present after it; this bread and this cup were distinguished from the meal itself by the solemn declaration over them of the fact of the institution. The entire feast, however, had a solemnity and sanctity imparted to it by the eucharistic acts which accompanied it, Ellicott says, and while this bread and this wine constituted the Supper of the Lord, the entire charity-feast became consecrated by it as a Lord's Supper, the phrase being similar to Lord's day. To it the brethren came, not as individuals, but as members of the body of Christ, Ellicott says: this gathering of the Church was his body now on earth, and that sacramental bread and wine were the symbols of his body which had been on earth and had been given for them; to the charity-feast the rich brought of their abundance and the poor of their poverty, but once assembled there everything was common. The party spirit which raged outside soon invaded these sacred scenes, Ellicott says: the rich members ceased to discern in that gathering the Body, and to discern themselves as members of that Body, regarding themselves as individuals and the food which they brought as their own, so that the poor were put to shame, some of them arriving late and remaining hungry while the rich had eaten and drunk to excess; and on those who acted thus there fell naturally God's judgments of sickness and of death. To correct this terrible evil and grave scandal St. Paul recalls to them the solemnity of the act of Holy Communion, what it meant and how it was instituted, Ellicott says, reminding them how the whole feast was consecrated by having that eucharistic bread and wine united with it, and commanding those who wanted merely to satisfy their natural hunger to do so at home before coming to the Lord's Supper. The two thoughts of communion with Christ and communion with one another, and of the bread and wine being the medium of the union with him and the source of the Christian unity, intersect and interlace each other, Ellicott says, like the fine threads of some tapestry which are so skilfully interwoven that you cannot distinguish them while you look on the image or scene which they definitely produce: we may with theological subtlety dissever them, but if we do so we shall lose that loving image of the Holy Communion which the Apostle wrought out in his teaching, and on which he and the early Church gazed with tender adoration, and from which they drew the deepest draughts of spiritual life. The words when I come contain no definite indication of an approaching visit, Ellicott concludes, being quite general, whenever I come. A.T. Robertson says that a sufficient number are already asleep in death because of their desecration of the Lord's table, that Paul evidently had knowledge of specific instances, and that a few would be too many. The condition in the next verse is of the second class, determined as unfulfilled, Robertson says, assuming that they had not been judging themselves discriminatingly, else they would not be judged, and there is a distinction to be noted in the two verbs. On being chastened of the Lord, Robertson says the verb comes from the word for a child and means to train a child, to discipline with words, to chastise with scourges, and so by afflictions as here; afflictions are meant to separate us from the doom of the wicked world. Albert Barnes says the weakness, sickness and death among them were judgments sent in consequence of their profanation of the ordinance, and that the design of such chastisement is expressly stated to be preventive, that they should not be condemned with the world; and that the closing directions require them to wait for one another and to satisfy hunger at home, so that the assembly may be for the ordinance and not for a meal.

debates: Whether the sickness and death were natural or sent: Clarke says it is hard to decide between the consequences of their own intemperance and disorders inflicted immediately by God, observing that experience shows many fall victims to intemperance; Ellicott allows both channels, that death sometimes resulted either naturally or by God's direct visitation; Robertson treats it as fact, that a sufficient number are already asleep in death and that Paul evidently knew specific instances; Gill, Wesley and Barnes take it simply as divine chastisement

What tarry one for another commands: Clarke and Calvin take it as requiring that all partake together and that the sacrament be separated from any common meal; Lightfoot guards it against a possible misuse, denying that the apostle is telling the Gentile part of the church to wait while the Jewish part eats its paschal ante-suppers, since he has already condemned those outright, and holding that the aim is to remove all dividing into parties

What the rest that Paul will set in order means: Calvin allows either that other matters needed better arrangement or that none did, since a man judges better when present, but attacks the interpretation which finds the mass promised here, asking what resemblance it bears to the institution Paul has just approved, and concluding that only outward decorum is meant, which lies in the Church's power to arrange by times, places and persons; Ellicott takes it as further details of the charity-feasts and notes that the words when I come indicate no particular visit

How the judgment is to be understood: Ellicott says the verse explicitly declares the condemnation was not final but temporal suffering, to save them from being condemned with the heathen; Robertson derives the verb from the word for a child and makes afflictions the means of separating us from the doom of the world; Clarke makes the escape conditional on self-condemnation and humbling
outliers: Clarke's quotation of the Communion service, that such conduct might provoke God to plague men with divers diseases and sundry kinds of death
Robertson's remark that a few deaths would be too many, and that Paul evidently had specific instances in view
Ellicott's reconstruction of the apostolic rite, from the Greek contributory feast through the charity-feast to a Supper of two parts, a loaf broken during the meal and a cup taken after it
Ellicott's observation that the phrase Lord's Supper is formed like Lord's day, the whole feast being consecrated by the eucharistic acts within it
Ellicott's closing image of communion with Christ and communion with one another interwoven like the threads of a tapestry, which theological subtlety may dissever only at the cost of the picture
